nuance.usage_note: Negator is used mainly in linguistics, logic and computing, where it names a word or operator that makes a statement negative. Ordinary Americans say 'not' or 'negation word' instead. In a grammar or logic class, you might hear 'the negator in this sentence is never'.

distinctions.note: Negation is the process or the result of making something negative; a negator is the element that performs it.
Negative as an adjective describes a value or statement that is not affirmative; negator names the device that produces that value.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked what the negator is in 'I don't know', and I told her it's the word 'not' hidden inside 'don't'.
examples.professional: In the query parser, the negator field tells the engine which token flips the boolean value of the filter.
examples.analytical: In Aristotle's logic, the negator 'not' transforms a predicate into its contradictory, so that 'is just' becomes 'is not just'.

nuance.analogy: A negator is like a mirror-flip button in a photo editor: one click reverses the image, but the content stays the same.
nuance.etymology: From negate, from Latin negare 'to deny', plus the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Confusing negator with negotiator, which is a person who bargains.
Using negator for a person who is pessimistic; in that sense, say 'a pessimist' or 'a naysayer'.

senses.definition: The transfer of impulses between neurons.

core.definition: The passing of chemical or electrical signals between nerve cells across the synapse, which lets neurons communicate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MISH, not on neuro, and the last syllable is a weak uh. Keep the r in NOOR, and do not turn the ending into mee-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise scientific term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in neuroscience, medicine, psychology and biology courses, and in research papers. In everyday talk people say brain signals or nerve signals, and neurotransmitter is more common than neurotransmission in conversation. Use the longer word when you need to name the process itself rather than the chemical messenger.

distinctions.note: A neurotransmitter is the chemical that carries the signal, while neurotransmission is the whole process of passing it along.
Synaptic transmission names signal passing across a synapse specifically, while neurotransmission is the broader term for all neural signaling.
Neuromodulation refers to slower, broader adjustments of neural activity, whereas neurotransmission is the fast, direct transfer of a signal.

examples.everyday: Some medications change your mood because they interfere with neurotransmission in the brain.
examples.professional: Our model estimates the neurotransmission delay from the spike-timing data we recorded last month.
examples.analytical: Any philosophy of mind must reckon with how neurotransmission grounds the chemistry of thought in physical processes.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay runner passing a baton across a short gap to a teammate.
nuance.etymology: From Greek neuron (nerve) plus transmission, from Latin transmittere (to send across).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in NOO-ro-trans-mish-un; the main stress belongs on MISH.
Confusing it with neurotransmitter, which names the chemical rather than the process.

senses.definition: Precisely; with fine discernment or judgment.
senses.example: The judge worded the ruling nicely, so every clause left no room for doubt.

senses.definition: Pleasantly; satisfactorily.

core.definition: In a pleasant, satisfactory, or well-done way; well. Often used to say something turned out well or was done properly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Keep the s of nice clear and do not slide it into a z, and say the final -ly as a short, light lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Used in praise or to describe something going well, though it can sound vague or childish when used to tell someone to behave.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nicely constantly in everyday speech, especially to say something is going well (Things are going nicely) or to praise work (That was nicely done). When used to a child, Please say it nicely means politely or pleasantly. A natural reply to How are you doing? is Doing nicely, thanks.

distinctions.note: Well is the broadest adverb for doing something correctly or successfully; nicely adds the idea of pleasantness or neatness.
Fine is more casual and general; nicely suggests a result that is pleasant or particularly good.

examples.everyday: The kids are sleeping now, so the evening went nicely.
examples.professional: The migration to the new database went nicely, with only minor delays on the reporting team.
examples.analytical: The argument fits nicely with Augustine's account of desire, though it complicates his claim about the will.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned engine that runs smoothly without drawing attention to itself.
nuance.etymology: Nice (from Latin nescius, meaning ignorant) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using nice as an adverb, as in 'It went nice'; use nicely.
Using nicely to mean very or quite, as in 'nicely cold'; in American speech this sounds odd.

senses.definition: Initialism of natural-language understanding.
Initialism of not like us.
senses.example: My niece texted NLU after seeing the new neighbors' loud party on Friday night.

core.definition: Natural-language understanding: the AI task of getting a computer to work out the meaning and intent of human language.

pronunciation.tip: Say the three letters separately, N-L-U, with the strong stress on the final U, which sounds like the word 'you'. Do not say it as one word, like 'en-LOO'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term in AI and data work, and a slang tag on social media for the phrase 'not like us'.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers and data scientists use NLU constantly in meetings and documentation, usually next to NLP (natural-language processing) and NLG (natural-language generation). The phrase 'not like us' is internet slang, often used to mark someone as an outsider or to mock a group. Context usually makes clear which sense is meant.

distinctions.note: NLP is the broad field of computing with human language; NLU is the subfield focused on meaning and intent.
NLG produces text from data, while NLU interprets text that a person or system has written or said.

examples.everyday: My cousin works on NLU at a startup, so she's always complaining about chatbots that misunderstand people.
examples.professional: The NLU team needs to retrain the intent classifier before Friday's release.
examples.analytical: Strong scores on NLU benchmarks do not show that a system grasps meaning in any full human sense.

nuance.analogy: NLU is like an interpreter who figures out what a speaker actually means, not just which words were said.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'natural-language understanding', from 'natural language' (human speech, as opposed to code) plus 'understanding'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the letters as a single word, like 'en-LOO'
Using NLU for the whole field of language computing, when NLP is the broader term

senses.definition: A deleterious placebo effect.
senses.example: Half the patients who reported headaches felt them because of the nocebo effect, not the drug.

core.definition: Harm, such as pain, nausea or fatigue, caused by a patient's negative expectations rather than by a treatment's active chemistry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEE in nocebo and the second syllable of effect, which is a noun with stress on its second syllable. Keep the first word's middle syllable clear rather than reducing it to a weak sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes harm that is psychological in origin, often discussed in medical research.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nocebo effect in clinical and research discussions, for example when reporting side effects in drug trials. In everyday conversation, people say I think I'm feeling side effects just from worrying about them. Experts use the term carefully, because it describes real symptoms without a chemical cause.

distinctions.note: The placebo effect produces benefit through expectation, while the nocebo effect produces harm through expectation.
A side effect is caused by a drug's active chemistry, while a nocebo effect is caused by expectation.

examples.everyday: I got a headache just from reading the warning label, and I think that's the nocebo effect.
examples.professional: Our adverse-event report should separate true drug toxicity from the nocebo effect.
examples.analytical: The nocebo effect complicates medical ethics, since informing patients of risks can itself create the harms described.

nuance.analogy: A self-fulfilling prophecy in the body: expecting harm can help produce it.
nuance.etymology: From nocebo, Latin for I shall harm, plus effect.
common_mistakes: Confusing nocebo effect with side effect, which comes from a drug's chemistry.
Stressing the first syllable of effect when used as a noun, as in EF-fekt; the noun stress is on the second syllable.
Pronouncing nocebo as NOH-see-boh.

senses.definition: A word invented for the occasion, especially to create alliteration or a rhyme.

core.definition: A word coined for one occasion, often to create a rhyme or alliteration, that is not used again.

pronunciation.tip: Nonce sounds like nahns, with a short vowel and a clear s at the end. The stress falls on WORD, so the second word is louder; keep the r in WURD rather than dropping it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a linguistic term, though it can sound playful when used about someone's clever coinage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonce word mainly in linguistics, literature classes, and writing discussions. It describes a word made up for one joke, poem, or moment. Many nonce words spread beyond their origin, so a word can start as a nonce word and later become ordinary vocabulary.
word_family: nonce (noun, mainly in the phrase for the nonce, meaning for now)

distinctions.note: A neologism is a new word that may catch on and enter dictionaries; a nonce word is coined for one occasion and usually disappears.
A portmanteau blends two words, like brunch from breakfast and lunch; a nonce word may be a portmanteau, but any invented word can be a nonce word.

examples.everyday: Whenever my daughter invents a silly word for one joke, like glorpy, I call it a nonce word.
examples.professional: The tagline we wrote for this campaign is a nonce word, so we shouldn't add it to the brand glossary.
examples.analytical: Lewis Carroll's chortle, coined in Through the Looking-Glass, began as a nonce word and unexpectedly entered the language.

nuance.analogy: A nonce word is like a disposable paper cup: made for one occasion and thrown away, unless someone decides to keep it.
nuance.etymology: From the phrase for the nonce, from Middle English for than nones, meaning for the once.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing nonce as nonts or nonse; it has a short vowel and an s sound, NAHNS.
Using nonce word for any new word; it applies only to a word made for one occasion, not to a term that is widely adopted.

related: nonce (noun, mainly in the phrase for the nonce, meaning for now)

senses.definition: Letters or words, in writing or speech, that have no meaning or pattern or seem to have no meaning.
senses.example: After my father had a stroke, every time he tried to talk, it sounded like nonsense.

senses.definition: An untrue statement.
That which is silly, illogical and lacks any meaning, reason or value; that which does not make sense.
Something foolish; tomfoolery.
senses.example: Stop the nonsense and tell me where you actually left the car keys.

senses.definition: A type of poetry that contains strange or surreal ideas, as, for example, that written by Edward Lear.
senses.example: Our seminar spent a week on Victorian nonsense, including Edward Lear's limericks.

senses.definition: A damaged DNA sequence whose products are not biologically active, that is, that does nothing.
senses.example: The sequencing revealed a nonsense in the gene, so the protein was never produced.

senses.definition: To make nonsense of;
senses.example: The new evidence made nonsense of the prosecution's theory entirely.

senses.definition: To attempt to dismiss as nonsense; to ignore or belittle the significance of something; to render unimportant or puny.
senses.example: Don't nonsense my concerns just because the budget is tight.

senses.definition: To joke around, to waste time.
senses.example: We spent the afternoon nonsensing in the break room instead of working.

senses.definition: Nonsensical.
senses.example: The nonsense explanation for the delayed flight made no sense to anyone.

senses.definition: Resulting from the substitution of a nucleotide in a sense codon, causing it to become a stop codon (not coding for an amino-acid).
senses.example: Researchers identified a nonsense mutation that cut the protein short.

senses.definition: An emphatic rejection of something one has just heard and does not believe or agree with.
senses.example: Nonsense! Those numbers can't possibly be right, I checked them twice.

core.definition: Words or ideas that are silly, illogical, or meaningless; something that does not make sense or is untrue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NON. The second syllable is full, not reduced: say 'sens' with a short e, not 'sunss' or 'suhns.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling something nonsense is a dismissive judgment, and it can sound rude or confrontational when used about a person's ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nonsense' very often in casual conversation to dismiss an idea or claim, as in 'That's nonsense!' It can sound harsh if you say it directly to someone's face, so a softer alternative is 'I don't think that's right.' The word is uncountable in general use, but 'a piece of nonsense' is a natural way to refer to one specific silly claim. As an interjection, 'Nonsense!' expresses friendly disagreement, often used by older people.

distinctions.note: 'Gibberish' refers to meaningless speech or sounds, often unintelligible, while 'nonsense' can also refer to ideas that are silly or false but still grammatical.
'Rubbish' is mainly British for 'trash' or for nonsense; Americans say 'garbage,' 'trash,' or 'nonsense' instead.
A lie is a deliberate falsehood, while nonsense is simply illogical or untrue, with no suggestion of intent to deceive.

examples.everyday: That's total nonsense, Mike, the store is definitely open on Sundays.
examples.professional: The slide that claims the model improved by 300 percent is nonsense, so we should remove it before the review.
examples.analytical: Dismissing a theological argument as nonsense without identifying its premises is a rhetorical move, not a refutation.

nuance.analogy: Nonsense is like a sentence that looks well-built but has no foundation: the words stand up, yet the house falls down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin non sensus, 'not sense.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'a nonsense' as a countable noun without a phrase; say 'a piece of nonsense' or 'that's nonsense' instead.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a reduced 'suns' rather than a clear 'sens.'

senses.definition: A function which satisfies a particular set of formal conditions, created to generalize the notion of the length of a vector. Formally, a real-valued function on a vector space, generally denoted v↦|v| or v↦‖v‖, that satisfies the following properties:
senses.example: In functional analysis, every Banach space comes equipped with a norm that induces its topology.

senses.definition: Any of several generalizations of the above: a field norm, ideal norm, etc.
senses.example: A quaternion algebra (a,b) over ksplits if and only if b is a norm from the field extension k(a)/k, i.e. if and only if there is some x in k(a) which has field norm exactly equal to b.

senses.definition: An element of the image of some (generalized) norm, the element then said to be from the norm in question, or from the structure which gave rise to the norm.
senses.example: A quaternion algebra (a,b) over ksplits if and only if b is a norm from the field extension k(a)/k, i.e. if and only if there is some x in k(a) which has field norm exactly equal to b.

senses.definition: That which is normal or typical.
senses.example: Unemployment is the norm in this part of the country.

senses.definition: A rule that is imposed by regulations and/or socially enforced by members of a community.
senses.example: Not eating your children is just one of those societal norms.

senses.definition: A sentence with non-descriptive meaning, such as a command, permission, or prohibition.
senses.example: Philosophers distinguish descriptive statements from norms, which tell us what ought to happen.

senses.definition: If v≠0 then ‖v‖≠0;
senses.example: A norm must return a nonzero value for every nonzero vector.

senses.definition: Given a scalar k, ‖kv‖=|k|⋅‖v‖, where |k| is the absolute value of k;
senses.example: Scaling a vector by k multiplies its norm by the absolute value of k.

senses.definition: Given two vectors v,w, ‖v+w‖≤‖v‖+‖w‖ (the triangle inequality).
senses.example: The triangle inequality says the norm of a sum never exceeds the sum of norms.

senses.definition: A high level of performance in a chess tournament, several of which are required for a player to receive a title.
senses.example: He needed one more norm against grandmasters to earn the title.

senses.definition: To endow (a vector space, etc.) with a norm.
senses.example: Mathematicians often norm the space so that distances can be measured consistently.

core.definition: A standard or typical way people behave or things are done, often unwritten, that a group expects others to follow.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with an open vowel like the 'aw' of 'law,' and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech. Don't add an extra vowel and say 'nor-um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a norm describes what is expected, though 'social norms' can sound restrictive when criticized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use norm in everyday talk and in social science; 'the norm' means what is typical, as in 'Remote work is the norm now.' Plural forms like 'social norms' and 'cultural norms' are common. In casual speech 'usual' or 'the way things are' may sound more natural.

distinctions.note: A rule is explicit and often written; a norm is an expected pattern of behavior that may never be written down.
A standard is a formal, measurable benchmark often set by an authority; a norm is an informal group expectation.
A custom is a traditional practice in a community; a norm can be broader, such as the expected way to act at work.

examples.everyday: It's the norm around here to bring a dish when you visit someone for dinner.
examples.professional: Our team follows industry norms for code reviews, so every change gets a second look before it merges.
examples.analytical: Sociologists argue that shared norms make everyday cooperation possible even where no law requires it.

nuance.analogy: Norms are the unwritten rules of a group, like people lining up for coffee in order without a sign telling them to.
nuance.etymology: From Latin norma, 'carpenter's square' or 'rule,' via French norme.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in norm' or 'as a norm' to mean 'as usual'; the natural phrase is 'the norm' or 'normally.'
Confusing norm with normal; norm is the standard, while normal is the adjective describing something typical.

norm.etymology: From Latin *norma* (“a carpenter's square, a rule, a pattern, a precept”).

senses.definition: An officer who can administer oaths and statutory declarations, witness and authenticate documents and perform certain other acts varying from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.
senses.example: The bank required my signature to be witnessed by a notary public before approving the mortgage documents.

core.definition: An official authorized to witness signatures, administer oaths and certify documents, usually without giving legal advice.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed in careful speech, with the strongest stress on 'NOH' and 'PUB'. In quick speech the first 'notary' is often reduced to 'NOH-tuh-ree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names an official role used in everyday legal paperwork.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'notary' alone in conversation, but the full term 'notary public' appears on stamps, forms and signs. You might ask a bank or shipping store, 'Do you have a notary public here?' Notaries are commissioned by states, so their rules and limits vary by state.

distinctions.note: A lawyer can give legal advice and represent clients in court; a notary public typically cannot.
In Britain, 'notary' often means a lawyer with special authority, so the US notary public is a different role.

collocations: in front of a notary public

examples.everyday: The bank has a notary public on Tuesdays if you need something signed.
examples.professional: Please have the signatory appear in front of a notary public before we file the agreement.
examples.analytical: The notary public's authority is statutory, so its scope varies from state to state.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who checks that the players are who they say they are before the match starts.
nuance.etymology: 'Notary' from Latin notarius; 'public' from Latin publicus, 'of the people', from populus.
common_mistakes: Believing that a US notary public can give legal advice or act as a lawyer.
Writing the plural as 'notary publics' instead of 'notaries public'.

notary-public.etymology: Anglo-Norman/Law French, on model of *notaire publique*, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun, instead of idiomatic English *public notary.

senses.definition: Sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (also called top-p sampling).

core.definition: A method for generating text in which the model samples only from the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to a threshold p.

pronunciation.tip: The word nucleus is stressed on its first syllable, while sampling has primary stress on SAM. In fast speech, the final 's' of 'nucleus' often blends into the 'nu' sound, so it sounds like 'nu-klee-us SAM-pling'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in machine learning discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nucleus sampling mainly among machine learning engineers and researchers discussing how language models choose their next word. It is usually explained as top-p sampling, and it is compared with top-k sampling. It is not used in everyday conversation, and it should be introduced with a brief definition when speaking to non-specialists.

distinctions.note: Top-k keeps a fixed number of the most likely tokens, while nucleus sampling keeps a varying set whose probabilities reach p.
Greedy decoding always picks the single most probable token, while nucleus sampling introduces randomness within a probability threshold.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the chatbot sounds more natural because it uses nucleus sampling.
examples.professional: Let's switch the generation settings to nucleus sampling with p equal to 0.9 and compare the output quality.
examples.analytical: Nucleus sampling trades a degree of determinism for diversity by truncating the tail of the distribution adaptively at each step.

nuance.analogy: Nucleus sampling is like choosing a team from the people who make up most of the candidate pool, while ignoring the long tail of unlikely candidates.
nuance.etymology: Nucleus is from Latin, 'kernel'; the term was adopted in machine learning for a sampling method that keeps the core of the probability mass.
common_mistakes: Confusing nucleus sampling with top-k sampling and assuming both use a fixed number of tokens.
Stressing nucleus on its second syllable instead of the first.

conversation.text: Nucleus sampling picks from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p.
Unlike top-k, nucleus sampling adapts: the candidate set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it isn't.
Nucleus sampling with p set to 0.9 is a common default for open-ended generation.

senses.definition: In an obdurate manner; stubbornly, intractably or inflexibly.
senses.example: The senator obdurately refused to revisit the tax bill, even after the economists objected.

core.definition: In a stubborn way that refuses to change one's mind, even under pressure or when given good reasons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AHB. The 'ur' is r-colored in General American, and the final -ly is a light 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes stubbornness that refuses to yield, which is usually seen as a flaw.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obdurately mainly in writing or formal speech, such as news reports, opinion pieces, or an academic argument. In casual talk, people say 'stubbornly' or 'dig in their heels.' It is a strong word, so use it carefully about a person, since it can sound harsh.

distinctions.note: Stubbornly is the everyday American word and is less intense. Obdurately implies a harder, more formal refusal to yield.
Obstinately stresses persistence in a course of action, sometimes a mistaken one. Obdurately stresses a hard refusal to be moved by reasons or pressure.
Intractably describes problems or people that are very hard to manage or resolve, while obdurately describes a deliberate refusal to yield.

examples.everyday: My brother obdurately refused to admit he had taken the wrong exit, even after we passed the same gas station twice.
examples.professional: The vendor obdurately refused to revise the contract, even after three rounds of feedback from our legal team.
examples.analytical: Kant's critics obdurately insisted that moral law must be grounded in experience, and so missed the force of his argument for a priori reason.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone in a stream: the water keeps pushing, but the stone does not move.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obdurare, to harden, from ob- (against) and durare (to last or harden).
common_mistakes: Confusing obdurate with durable. Durable means long-lasting, while obdurate means stubborn.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: In an obedient manner.

core.definition: In a way that does what one is told, following instructions, orders or rules without resisting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -BEE-. The -ient ending is reduced to 'ee-uhnt,' so it sounds like 'oh-BEE-dee-uhnt-lee' with no hard 't' sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a good quality in children, pets and employees, but it can suggest submissiveness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obediently for pets, children, soldiers and employees, often in stories or reports. In casual talk, people more often say 'the dog sat right down' or 'she did what she was told.' The word can sound a little stiff in conversation, so use it when you are describing behavior in writing or in a formal report.

distinctions.note: Dutifully implies a sense of moral duty or responsibility. Obediently simply describes following orders.
Compliantly suggests going along with a request, often reluctantly or without thinking. Obediently suggests a more consistent habit of following authority.

examples.everyday: The puppy sat down obediently when I said stay, which surprised everyone at the park.
examples.professional: The new hires obediently followed the onboarding checklist without asking why each step mattered.
examples.analytical: Milgram's participants continued to administer what they believed were shocks, obediently following instructions from an authority figure.

nuance.analogy: Like a train on its tracks: it goes exactly where the rails lead.
nuance.etymology: From obedient, from Latin oboedire (to listen to, obey), plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using obedient as an adverb. Use obediently to describe how someone acts.
Misspelling it as obediantly. The vowel in the middle is e.

senses.definition: Extremely overweight, especially: weighing more than 20% (for men) or 25% (for women) over their conventionally ideal weight determined by height and build; or, having a body mass index over 30 kg/m.
senses.example: The doctor said the patient was obese and needed a diabetes screening.

senses.definition: A person who is obese.
senses.example: Researchers found that most of the obese participants had never been offered any treatment.

core.definition: Extremely overweight, with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, to a degree that poses serious health risks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BEES. The final s is a voiceless 's', not a 'z', and the first syllable is 'oh' as in 'go'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical; it can be hurtful in casual conversation, so Americans often prefer 'overweight' or 'living with obesity' in polite settings.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, health reports, and government statistics use 'obese' as a medical category. In everyday talk, Americans often avoid it because it sounds harsh and stigmatizing. Saying 'overweight' is usually more polite, but 'obese' is common in health contexts.

distinctions.note: Overweight is a milder term for a BMI of 25 to 29.9; obese is a stronger medical category for a BMI of 30 or higher.
Fat is blunt and informal, and often considered rude; obese is clinical and more precise.

examples.everyday: My doctor said I'm not obese, but I should lose a few pounds to lower my blood pressure.
examples.professional: The study tracks how many obese adults in the sample develop type 2 diabetes over ten years.
examples.analytical: Defining obesity by BMI alone raises questions about whether a single numerical threshold can fairly describe health across different body compositions.

nuance.analogy: Obese is like a warning light on a car dashboard: it does not describe the whole engine, but it signals that something needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obesus, 'eaten away, stout', from obedere, 'to eat up'.
common_mistakes: Using obese as a casual insult; it sounds harsh and can be hurtful.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ob' as in 'obey'; it is 'oh-BEES'.

obese.etymology: From Latin *obēsus*, derived from *obedō* (“to devour, eat away”), from *ob* (“away”) + *edō* (“to eat”).

senses.definition: Under an obligation to do something.
senses.example: All employees are obliged to complete a tax return every year.

senses.definition: Grateful or indebted because of a favor done.
senses.example: I'm greatly obliged for your help with this problem.

core.definition: Grateful for a favor someone did for you, or bound by duty to do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BLYJE. The final -ged is pronounced as a single d sound, so the word ends in 'blyjd' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means grateful; neutral or negative when it means being forced to act.
nuance.usage_note: Common in American phrases like 'I'd be much obliged' or 'Much obliged!', which mean thank you. These are a bit old-fashioned or folksy and are often heard in the South and rural areas. In formal email, 'We would be obliged if you could...' is polite. For everyday thanks, 'Thanks so much' is more usual.

distinctions.note: Obligated is about duty or commitment; obliged can also mean grateful, as in 'I'm obliged to you'.
Grateful expresses thanks directly; obliged often sounds more formal or folksy, and it can also mean required.

examples.everyday: Thanks for holding the door for me, I'm much obliged.
examples.professional: We would be obliged if you could send the signed contract by Friday.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a person who has been helped feels obliged to return the kindness, even without a contract.

nuance.analogy: Being obliged is like carrying a borrowed umbrella: you feel you owe something back, even if no one asked for it.
nuance.etymology: From oblige, from Latin obligare, to bind; the adjective keeps both the senses of duty and gratitude.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'm obliged' to mean 'okay' or 'I agree'; it means thanks or duty
Using 'obliged' for a casual please; it is not a polite request word in everyday speech
Confusing 'obliged' with 'obligated' when you mean grateful

senses.definition: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)
senses.example: The rare birds lived under constant observation by the research team, who never let them see it.

senses.definition: The act of noting and recording some event; or the record of such noting.
senses.example: Her nightly observation log recorded the temperature and wind speed every fifteen minutes.

senses.definition: A remark or comment.
senses.example: He offered a sharp observation about the budget that nobody else in the meeting had noticed.

senses.definition: A judgment based on observing.
senses.example: Her observation that the sample was contaminated proved correct once the lab results came back.

senses.definition: An evaluation conducted through observing.
senses.example: I need to do your observation before the end of the week.

senses.definition: Performance of what is prescribed; adherence in practice; observance.
senses.example: Strict observation of the Sabbath was expected in that household, and no one ever questioned it.

senses.definition: A regime under which a subject is routinely observed.
senses.example: After the suicide attempt, the nurses placed the patient on observation for the entire night.

senses.definition: A realization of a random variable.
senses.example: Each observation in the dataset is treated as an independent realization from the same distribution.

core.definition: The act of watching or noticing something carefully, or the notes or record of what was noticed.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on VAY, and the first syllable has a weak secondary stress. The ending -tion is said 'shun', with no separate vowel before the n. Americans say the 'ah' vowel in the first syllable, as in 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to the act of noticing and does not carry praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: In American meetings people often say 'I have one observation' before offering a comment, which sounds polite and professional. In medicine, a patient can be kept 'under observation' overnight, and in science 'observations' means recorded data. The word can also mean a remark, so 'I'd like to make an observation' is a common phrase.

distinctions.note: A comment is any spoken remark; an observation is a remark based on something you actually saw or noticed.
Observance means following a rule, custom or holy day; observation means watching or noticing.
Inspection is a formal check against a standard, while observation may be informal and simply noting what happens.

examples.everyday: My observation is that the bakery sells out by ten on Saturdays, so go early.
examples.professional: Based on my observation of the dashboard, the spike started right after the release.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that observation alone cannot justify our belief that one event causes another.

nuance.analogy: Like a field notebook: the observation is both the act of looking and the careful record that follows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin observatio, from observare 'to watch over, keep'.
common_mistakes: Using observation to mean religious observance; the Sabbath observance is a different word.
Treating observations as a countable plural in data contexts: say 'the observations were recorded', not 'the observation was recorded' when you mean many.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 17:20-21 the Pharisees ask when the kingdom of God will come, and Jesus answers that it does not come in a way that can be watched and recorded for signs. The Greek word here is paratēreisis, meaning close watching or scrutiny, which is what the Pharisees were practicing. In Matthew 16:1-4 the Pharisees ask for a sign, and Jesus rebukes them for being able to read the sky but not the signs of the times.

observation.etymology: From Middle English *observacion*, borrowed from Middle French *observacion*.

senses.definition: An immediate inference that denies the opposite of something previously affirmed.
senses.example: All men are mortal, so, by obversion, no men are immortal.

senses.definition: The act of turning toward or downward.
senses.example: The botanist noted the obversion of the leaves, which turned their undersides toward the sun.

core.definition: In logic, an immediate inference that turns a statement into an equivalent one by changing its quality and negating its predicate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable 'vur.' The ending '-sion' is pronounced 'zhun' after the r in this word, so avoid saying 'ob-VER-shun.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in logic without emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter obversion mainly in philosophy and logic courses, often alongside conversion and contraposition. Outside of those fields, the word is almost never used. The second sense, turning toward or downward, is rare and mostly archaic.

distinctions.note: Conversion swaps the subject and predicate of a statement. Obversion changes the quality of the statement and negates the predicate, without swapping terms.
Contraposition swaps and negates both terms. Obversion keeps the same terms in their original order and only changes the quality and the predicate.

examples.everyday: My logic professor said that obversion turns 'all dogs are animals' into 'no dogs are non-animals,' which still means the same thing.
examples.professional: The rules engine applies obversion before matching, so the negated condition is written in a standard form.
examples.analytical: Obversion preserves logical equivalence, which is why it counts as an immediate inference rather than a new premise.

nuance.analogy: Like rewriting a sign that says 'open' as 'not closed,' obversion keeps the meaning while flipping the wording.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obversio, 'a turning toward,' from obvertere, 'to turn toward or against.'
common_mistakes: Confusing obversion with conversion, which swaps terms.
Mispronouncing the ending as 'shun' instead of 'zhun.'

senses.definition: A grammatical marker that distinguishes a relatively non-salient referent in a given context from a relatively salient (proximate) one.
senses.example: In the Algonquian grammar, the obviative marks a secondary third-person referent in the narrative.

senses.definition: Relating to such a referent or grammatical marker.
senses.example: The linguist noted that the obviative form appears only when two third-person characters interact.

core.definition: A grammatical form marking a less prominent third-person referent, distinguishing it from the main, proximate one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHB. The ending is reduced to 'uh-tiv' with a schwa, not 'ay-tiv,' and the word has four syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is precise and used only in linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist term from linguistics, especially the study of Algonquian languages such as Cree and Ojibwe. Americans outside linguistics will almost never use it. As an adjective, obviative describes a referent or a form that carries this marking.

distinctions.note: Obviate is a verb meaning to prevent or remove a need, and it is a separate word that is not related in meaning to the grammatical sense of obviative.
Proximate names the more prominent, central referent in a discourse, while obviative names the less prominent one.

examples.everyday: I'm reading about the obviative in Ojibwe; it's how speakers keep track of who is who in a story.
examples.professional: In our fieldwork report, we mark the obviative on the secondary participant so the transcript stays clear.
examples.analytical: The obviative distinguishes the less topical referent, which lets the speaker maintain reference across shifting participants.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage direction telling the audience which actor is the main character.
nuance.etymology: A term from Algonquian linguistics, probably built on Latin obvius 'in the way.'
common_mistakes: Confusing obviative with obviate, which is a common verb.
Using obviative as a general word for something obvious.

senses.definition: Away from a main location; in a place not owned by a particular organization.
senses.example: The team held its annual planning retreat at an offsite conference center in Vermont.

senses.definition: Away from a particular site.
senses.example: Several employees worked offsite on Fridays, so the office was often quiet.

senses.definition: A group outing or meeting that takes place outside of the office.
senses.example: They went bowling for their team offsite.

core.definition: Located away from the main workplace, such as at a hotel, another building, or a retreat venue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OFF, with a lighter stress on SITE. The word 'site' rhymes with 'light' and has the long i of 'bite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals a change of setting for a meeting, event, or project.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'offsite' means a meeting or retreat held somewhere away from the usual workplace, such as a hotel or a lake house. It is common in emails and meeting invitations. Use 'remote' for people working from home, and use 'offsite' for events or locations.

distinctions.note: Remote describes working from home or from anywhere, while offsite refers to a location away from the office for meetings or work.
Off-campus is used for schools and universities; offsite is the common business term.

examples.everyday: Next week the whole team is going to an offsite at a lake house.
examples.professional: Let's move the planning discussion to an offsite session so we can focus without interruptions.
examples.analytical: An offsite location separates an organization's decisions from its daily routines, which changes how people reason about them.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a board game to the park: the same pieces, but a different table.
nuance.etymology: Compound of off and site, meaning away from the site.
common_mistakes: Writing 'off site' as two words in formal memos; the one-word form is standard in business writing.
Using offsite to mean remote, as in an employee working from home.

conversation.text: The leadership team is at an offsite in Napa all week.
We're planning a two-day offsite to work on next year's strategy.
Let's save the big-picture discussion for the offsite.

senses.definition: Having very strong opinions.
senses.example: Her dad is so opinionated that when he's around it is hard to simply relax and have a light conversation.

senses.definition: Holding to one's own opinion obstinately and unreasonably.
senses.example: Her dad is so opinionated that the others' preferences were overridden and no one had any fun on the outing.

senses.definition: Infused with opinions rather than wholly objective.
senses.example: His essay was opinionated, which was a problem because the assignment had been to write a factual analysis.

senses.definition: Enforcing one particular approach instead of offering options and flexibility.
senses.example: an opinionated framework

core.definition: Having strong opinions and expressing them forcefully, often without much openness to other views.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PIN. The -ated ending is pronounced 'ay-tid', with the final vowel reduced to a short 'i' sound, not 'ayted'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative, suggesting stubbornness or arrogance; it can be neutral or mildly positive when describing someone with well-thought-out convictions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use opinionated to describe people who argue a lot or dismiss other views, such as a talk show host or a relative at dinner. It is a fairly direct criticism, so use it carefully. A softer alternative is 'has strong views' or 'knows what they think'.

distinctions.note: Outspoken means speaking openly and frankly, often positively; opinionated suggests being inflexible about one's views.
Stubborn describes refusing to change one's mind or behavior; opinionated focuses on strongly holding and voicing views.

examples.everyday: My uncle is very opinionated, so he'll argue with anyone about football.
examples.professional: Our product lead is brilliant but opinionated, so we should hear her out and then test her assumptions.
examples.analytical: The essay is opinionated rather than balanced, since the author dismisses every rival reading without engaging its evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio that only tunes to one station and turns down every other signal.
nuance.etymology: From opinion (from Latin opinio) plus the adjective suffix -ated, from Latin -atus.
common_mistakes: Spelling it opinioned, which is incorrect.
Using opinionated to mean simply 'having an opinion', when it implies strong or inflexible views.

senses.definition: In AI: The algorithm that updates a model's parameters during training, such as stochastic gradient descent or Adam.
A compiler or assembler that produces optimized code.
senses.example: The compiler's optimizer rewrote the loop so the program ran nearly twice as fast.

senses.definition: A program that uses linear programming to optimize a process.
senses.example: Our logistics team used an optimizer to find the cheapest delivery routes for the fleet.

senses.definition: A person in a large business whose task is to maximize profits and make the business more efficient.
senses.example: The company hired a cost optimizer to cut waste and streamline every department's budget.

core.definition: In machine learning, the algorithm that updates a model's parameters during training to reduce its error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'my' in the middle as a full diphthong. The final '-er' is a reduced rhotic 'er' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term that carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Machine learning engineers and data scientists use 'optimizer' every day, often naming specific ones such as Adam or SGD. Outside technical work, the word is rarely used. In programming tools, it can also mean a compiler component that makes code run faster, so the context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Optimization' is the process; 'optimizer' is the algorithm or component that carries it out.
A loss function measures error; the optimizer uses that measure to adjust the model's weights.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says the optimizer choice matters more than people think.
examples.professional: We switched the optimizer to Adam, and the training loss dropped much faster in the first epoch.
examples.analytical: The choice of optimizer shapes which minima a network converges to, so the inductive bias is partly an algorithmic decision.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who checks the slope under their feet and takes a step downhill, again and again, until they reach a valley.
nuance.etymology: From 'optimize' with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'optimizer' with 'optimization' when talking about the process rather than the algorithm.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'air' instead of a reduced 'er.'

conversation.text: The optimizer decides how to update the weights from the gradients; Adam and SGD are common choices.
Remember to reset the optimizer state when you load new weights for fine-tuning.

senses.definition: A shrine dedicated to some prophetic deity.
senses.example: Pilgrims traveled for days to reach the oracle at Delphi, the sacred shrine of Apollo.

senses.definition: A person such as a priest through whom the deity is supposed to respond with prophecies or advice.
senses.example: The oracle spoke only after the priestess inhaled the vapors from the temple floor.

senses.definition: A prophetic response, often enigmatic or allegorical, so given.
senses.example: King Croesus misread the oracle's answer and lost his entire kingdom in battle.

senses.definition: A person considered to be a source of wisdom.
senses.example: a literary oracle

senses.definition: A wise sentence or decision of great authority.
senses.example: Her grandmother's advice about never lending money to family became an oracle in our house.

senses.definition: A fortune-teller.
senses.example: The street oracle at the county fair promised me fame and a long marriage.

senses.definition: One who communicates a divine command; an angel; a prophet.
senses.example: In the old sermon, the oracle descended from heaven to warn Joseph in a dream.

senses.definition: The sanctuary, or most holy place in the temple; also, the temple itself.
senses.example: Only the high priest could enter the oracle, the innermost chamber of the temple.

senses.definition: A theoretical entity capable of answering some collection of questions.
senses.example: Turing imagined an oracle that could instantly answer any question about a given machine's behavior.

senses.definition: A third-party service that provides smart contracts with information from the outside world.
senses.example: The smart contract queried a price oracle to fetch the current exchange rate.

core.definition: A person or sacred place through which a god was believed to give authoritative answers, predictions, or advice; a trusted source of wise guidance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r strong. The final -cle is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so say OR-uh-kul in two beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; can be humorous when someone is jokingly called the oracle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oracle for someone whose knowledge is trusted, like the office oracle for computer problems, often with light humor. In the literal sense it refers to ancient Greek shrines such as Delphi or to a prophetic message. Calling a friend the oracle is a compliment, but using it for a casual guess sounds overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: A prophet speaks a divine message as a person; an oracle can be the message itself or the shrine where it was given.
Expert describes skill; oracle implies a trusted authority whose answers seem almost mysterious.
Guru suggests spiritual teaching or a following; oracle focuses on answers and predictions.

examples.everyday: Ask Dana about the printer; she's the office oracle when it comes to tech problems.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is the oracle for the legacy billing system, so check with her before changing anything.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Delphic oracle gave ambiguous answers on purpose or because the questions were poorly phrased.

nuance.analogy: An oracle is like a weather forecaster whose forecasts people treat as final, even when the forecast is cryptic.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oraculum, from orare, 'to speak, pray'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable in the middle; say OR-uh-kul, not OR-uh-ku-ul.
Using oracle for any expert; the word implies authority and sometimes mystery.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word debir refers to the inner sanctuary of the temple, the most holy room where the ark was placed and where God's presence was believed to dwell. In 1 Kings 6:19 Solomon sets up the inner sanctuary for the ark of the covenant, and 1 Kings 8:6 describes the priests bringing the ark into that inner place. In the New Testament, the Greek word logion, meaning 'utterance' or 'oracle', appears in Romans 3:2, where Paul says the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God, and in Acts 7:38, where Stephen calls the law the living oracles given to Moses.

oracle.etymology: From Middle English *oracle*, from Old French *oracle*, from Latin *ōrāculum*.

senses.definition: A method of representing a language or the sounds of language by written symbols; spelling.
senses.example: Her essay was praised for its clear argument, though its orthography needed some careful checking.

senses.definition: A set of conventions for writing a language, including norms of spelling, capitalization, emphasis, hyphenation, punctuation, and word breaks.
The aspect of language study concerned with letters and their sequences in words; the study of spelling.
senses.example: My linguistics professor spent a whole week on English orthography and its many irregularities.

senses.definition: Synonym of orthographer (“someone knowledgeable in spelling rules”).
senses.example: The dictionary's orthography consulted on every entry to catch spelling errors before printing.

core.definition: The accepted system of spelling and writing a language, including its rules for letters, capitalization, and punctuation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THAH, the second syllable. The vowel in the first syllable is the American cot vowel, and the final -phy is pronounced as a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a system and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Everyday Americans say spelling or the way something is written. Orthography is used by teachers, linguists, editors, and software developers when discussing whole writing systems. It sounds formal, so keep it for professional or academic discussion.

distinctions.note: Spelling refers to individual words, while orthography refers to the whole system of writing conventions in a language.
Phonology studies a language's sound system, while orthography is the system of written symbols representing those sounds.

examples.everyday: Spanish is easy for me to read because its orthography matches the sounds so closely.
examples.professional: Our style guide sets the orthography for product names, so every writer capitalizes and spaces them the same way.
examples.analytical: English orthography preserves spellings from earlier pronunciations, so the written form reveals the history of the language.

nuance.analogy: Orthography is like the rulebook for a game, while the words are the moves people make on the board.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orthographia, meaning correct writing, from orthos (correct) and graphein (to write).
common_mistakes: Misplacing the stress, as in or-THOG-ruh-fee, instead of or-THAH-gruh-fee.
Confusing orthography with orthodoxy, which means correct belief in religion or doctrine.

senses.definition: See other (determiner) below.
senses.example: Pick up the phone and find out who's on the other end.

senses.definition: Second.
senses.example: I get paid every other week.

senses.definition: Alien.
senses.example: The strange other lurked beyond the rift, watching our ship with glowing eyes.

senses.definition: Different.
senses.example: Our approach to the problem is other than the method in the textbook.

senses.definition: An other, another (person, etc), more often rendered as another.
senses.example: I'm afraid little Robbie does not always play well with others.

senses.definition: The other one; the second of two.
senses.example: One boat is not better than the other.

senses.definition: Not the one or ones previously referred to.
senses.example: Earning less than $2,000 a month, I have no other source of income except for gifts from relatives.

senses.definition: To regard, label, or treat as an "other", as not part of the same group; to view as different and alien.
senses.example: Critics argue that the media tends to other immigrants by portraying them as threats.

senses.definition: To treat as different or separate; segregate; ostracize.
senses.example: The clique quickly learned to other anyone who questioned their leader.

core.definition: Not the one or ones already mentioned or known; different from the one or ones before.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'th' is voiced, as in 'the', not as in 'thin'. The final syllable is a weak r-colored schwa, so do not say 'oh-ther' or 'uh-thair'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'other' before plural nouns, as in 'other people', and with 'the' before singular nouns, as in 'the other shoe'. To mean 'one more', say 'another' instead, as in 'another cup of coffee'. The word is also everywhere in phrases like 'on the other hand' and 'every other day', which people say naturally in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Another means one more of the same kind, while other refers to a different or remaining one.
Different describes a contrast in kind or quality, while other means not the one already mentioned.

examples.everyday: Can you pass me the other fork? This one still has food on it.
examples.professional: We'll ship the other two modules next sprint, after the API is stable.
examples.analytical: Kant treats other rational beings not as obstacles but as ends in themselves, which changes what respect requires.

nuance.analogy: Like the other shoe, the word points to the one not already in your hand.
nuance.etymology: From Old English óðer, meaning 'second of two'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'other coffee' when you mean 'another coffee'; use another for one more of a singular item.
Using 'other' alone for a plural noun with 'the', as in 'the other peoples' instead of 'the other people'.

other.etymology: From Middle English *other*, from Old English *ōþer* (“other, second”), from **ą̄þar*, **anþar*, from Proto-Germanic **anþeraz* (“other, second”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₂énteros* (“other”).

senses.definition: The area outside a racetrack or running track.
senses.example: The horses thundered past the grandstand, then drifted wide into the outfield.

senses.definition: The region of the field between the infield and the outer fence.
senses.example: He hit a long fly ball to the outfield in the gap to left.

senses.definition: The region of the field roughly outside of the infield or the wicket-keeper, slips, gully, point, cover, mid off, mid on, midwicket and square leg.
senses.example: The batter lofted the ball over the bowler's head, and it landed in the outfield for four.

senses.definition: To perform better in defense (fielding).
senses.example: Our team outfielded the visitors all afternoon and conceded only six runs.

core.definition: In baseball, the grassy part of the field beyond the infield, where the left fielder, center fielder and right fielder play.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, OUT, so it is 'OUT-field', not 'out-FIELD'. Don't drop the final d, and don't turn the vowel into 'oo' as in 'boot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, descriptive sports term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use outfield constantly when talking about baseball, both for the area and for the players collectively, as in 'our outfield is young.' Outside sports it is rarely used. The verb sense (to perform well in defense) is uncommon in everyday American speech, so you will mostly hear the noun. In cricket the word has a different meaning, so context matters.

distinctions.note: The infield is the diamond-shaped area inside the base paths, where the infielders play, while the outfield lies beyond it.
The warning track is the strip of dirt or gravel along the outfield wall, a narrow zone rather than the whole outfield.

collocations: a fly ball to the outfield

examples.everyday: My son is still learning to catch, so his coach always puts him in the outfield.
examples.professional: The stadium crew is replacing the outfield grass before the spring season, so the field will be closed for two weeks.
examples.analytical: The outfield's wide dimensions force defenders to cover ground that infielders rarely need to reach, which changes the defensive strategy.

nuance.analogy: The outfield is the big back yard of the baseball diamond, the wide grass where long hits go to be chased down.
nuance.etymology: A compound of out (away from the center) and field, from Old English ūt and feld.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (out-FIELD) instead of OUT-field.
Writing it as two words (out field) in formal writing.

senses.definition: A small likelihood; a remote possibility.

core.definition: A small or remote possibility that something will happen; a slim hope.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on chance, and outside is lighter but still clear. Say the ch as in church, and keep the ou as the ow diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly hopeful, but it always implies the outcome is unlikely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase to say something is possible but unlikely: 'There's an outside chance it snows tonight.' It is common in everyday talk and in news. It is usually followed by of plus a noun or gerund, as in an outside chance of winning. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I wouldn't count on it.'

distinctions.note: Slim chance means nearly the same and is equally informal, but slim stresses small size while outside stresses the far edge of possibility.
A long shot is an unlikely attempt or a competitor with little chance; outside chance describes the likelihood of an outcome.

examples.everyday: There's an outside chance the game gets rained out, so check the forecast before you go.
examples.professional: There's an outside chance the client signs by Friday, but I wouldn't build the plan around it.
examples.analytical: The hypothesis retains an outside chance of being correct, though the evidence now makes it very unlikely.

nuance.analogy: Like a parking space at the far edge of a packed lot: it exists, but it is unlikely to be free.
nuance.etymology: From outside, meaning at the far edge, plus chance; the phrase pictures a possibility at the margin of what is likely.
common_mistakes: Writing out side chance as separate words, or misspelling chance as change.
Using outside chance for a good chance; the phrase always means a remote possibility, so use good chance for likely outcomes.

senses.definition: Having been overstated; exaggerated; stated, displayed, or presented too grandly or prominently.
senses.example: The company's overstated claims about its battery life drew complaints from frustrated customers.

core.definition: Described or presented as bigger, stronger or more important than it really is; exaggerated.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OH in the adjective, with a weaker stress on STAY. The final -ed is a short 'id' sound here, so say 'tid' rather than 'tayt'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it implies that something has been exaggerated or inflated beyond the truth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to criticize claims in news, reports, reviews and debates: 'The benefits were overstated.' It is a measured word and sounds more professional than 'exaggerated' in workplace settings. Use it about claims, not people, so the criticism stays polite.

distinctions.note: Exaggerated is more general and can describe anything inflated, while overstated usually refers to claims, benefits, risks or importance.
Understated describes something presented more quietly or modestly than its real importance, which is the opposite of overstated.

examples.everyday: The ad said it would double your savings, but that was seriously overstated.
examples.professional: The vendor's overstated performance numbers made the project look more successful than it was.
examples.analytical: Many philosophical arguments about free will rest on overstated claims about what neuroscience has shown.

nuance.analogy: Like a photo with the colors turned up too high, the picture looks brighter than the real scene.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of overstate, from over- (beyond) plus state.
common_mistakes: Stressing STAYT instead of OH in the adjective, which sounds unnatural.
Using overstated to describe a person's character; it usually describes claims or statements.

senses.definition: A steam locomotive of the 4-6-2 wheel arrangement.
senses.example: We rode the old Pacific from Chicago to Denver, watching the prairie roll past the window.

senses.definition: Related to or located in the Pacific Ocean.

core.definition: Relating to the Pacific Ocean or to the countries, coasts and islands around it, including the western United States.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SIF, and reduce the first vowel to a schwa. Do not say 'PA-sih-fik' with a strong first syllable, which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a geographic term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word with a capital P for the ocean and the regions around it, such as Pacific Time, the Pacific Coast and the Pacific Northwest. Lowercase pacific means peaceful, which is a different word. In everyday speech, people often just say 'the Pacific' rather than 'the Pacific Ocean.'

distinctions.note: Lowercase pacific is a formal adjective meaning peaceful or inclined to peace, and it is unrelated to the ocean.
Atlantic refers to the ocean on the East Coast side of the United States, while Pacific refers to the ocean on the West Coast side.

examples.everyday: My sister lives on the Pacific coast, so she always calls me a few hours later in the day.
examples.professional: Our Pacific region team handles all of our West Coast customers, so please send those tickets to them.
examples.analytical: Pacific trade routes shaped the economic history of the American West Coast, linking ports to markets across Asia.

nuance.analogy: Pacific is like a large neighborhood on the far side of the country: a clear geographic label that tells you which edge of the map you mean.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pacificus, meaning peaceful or making peace; Magellan gave the ocean its name because his crossing was calm.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'PA-sih-fik'
Confusing Pacific with pacifist or pacific (lowercase) meaning peaceful
Forgetting the capital P when writing the name of the ocean or region

pacific.etymology: From Latin *pācificus* (“peace-making”), so called by Magellan because he sailed peacefully over it after weathering Cape Horn.

senses.definition: Having been placed in a package.
senses.example: The grocery store sells packaged salads that stay fresh in the refrigerator for a week.

core.definition: Sold in a box, bag, or sealed container, ready to buy without being measured or prepared.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PAK. The middle syllable is a reduced ih, and the ending -ged is pronounced as a single d sound, so say PAK-ijd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when describing food, since some people prefer fresh or homemade items. In business or shopping contexts it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use packaged for groceries and household items, such as packaged salad, packaged bread, or packaged snacks. It often appears in discussions of healthy eating, where some people prefer fresh foods. It is an everyday, neutral word used in stores and conversation.

distinctions.note: Prepackaged is a near synonym that stresses the item was packaged before it reached the store. Packaged is simpler and more common in everyday speech.
Fresh means recently harvested or made and not yet stored. Packaged means sold in a sealed container, which can be fresh or not.

examples.everyday: I usually buy packaged salad because it's faster than washing the lettuce myself.
examples.professional: The packaged software arrived pre-configured, so we skipped the custom installation and went live a week early.
examples.analytical: The essay criticizes packaged ideas that arrive ready-made, leaving readers no room to question their assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Packaged food is like a gift box already wrapped and tied: it's ready to hand over, but you cannot see the work that went into it.
nuance.etymology: From package, with the past participle ending -ed; package comes from pack with the suffix -age.
common_mistakes: Saying packaged with a long a sound or a second syllable like PAK-ih-jed.
Using packaged for something that is not sealed or pre-made, such as a box that you pack yourself.

senses.definition: The baptism of infants or young children.

core.definition: The Christian practice of baptizing infants and young children, as opposed to baptizing only people who profess faith.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable 'pae' is pronounced like 'pee', not 'pay'. Stress falls on BAP, and the final 'ism' is a reduced syllable, so say it as 'zum'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic theology, though the practice itself is contested among Christians, so the word can carry a debated or partisan feel in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: American theologians and seminary writers usually spell this word 'pedobaptism', while 'paedobaptism' is the older or British-influenced spelling. Both mean the same thing. In a church setting, Americans are more likely to say 'infant baptism' than use this technical term.

distinctions.note: Infant baptism is the plain, everyday term, while paedobaptism is a technical theological label used mainly in academic debates.
Credobaptism is the practice of baptizing only those who profess personal faith, which is the direct opposite of paedobaptism.

examples.everyday: My friend and I got into a long talk about baptizing babies, and she said the theological term for it is paedobaptism.
examples.professional: In this seminar, we will compare paedobaptism with believer's baptism and trace how each developed in the early church.
examples.analytical: The covenantal argument for paedobaptism depends on the continuity between circumcision in the Old Testament and baptism in the New, a claim its critics dispute.

nuance.analogy: Paedobaptism is like enrolling a child in a family's membership before the child can sign anything: the parents make the promise on the child's behalf, and the child later confirms it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'pais, paidos' meaning child, and 'baptismos' meaning baptism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'pay' rather than 'pee'.
Confusing paedobaptism with 'pedophilia', which has a completely different meaning and sounds alarming in English.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not use the word paedobaptism, but the debate centers on whether the household baptisms in Acts include children and whether baptism replaces circumcision. The Greek word 'baptizo' means to immerse or dip, and 'pais' means child or servant. Key passages include Acts 2:39, which speaks of the promise extending to children, Acts 16:33, which describes a jailer baptized with his whole family, and Colossians 2:11-12, which links baptism with circumcision.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church baptizes infants as a matter of course, immediately followed by chrismation and communion, which it sees as integral to full membership in the Church.

The Catholic Church baptizes infants, understanding baptism as the sacrament that removes original sin and incorporates the child into the Church, with godparents making promises on the child's behalf.

Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches practice infant baptism as a sign of God's covenant, while Baptist and most Pentecostal churches practice believer's baptism only, and Anabaptist-descended groups also reject infant baptism.

senses.definition: Relating to the baptism of infants or small children.
senses.example: The paedobaptist congregation baptized newborns within weeks of birth, as their tradition taught.

senses.definition: One who advocates for or practises infant baptism.

core.definition: A Christian who supports or practices baptizing infants and young children rather than only believing adults.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'pee' for the first syllable and stress the BAP syllable. The final 'ist' is short and clear, like the word 'ist' in 'Baptist'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic and church-history writing, though it can sound partisan when used to label someone in a dispute about baptism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this term in casual speech. In most American churches, people say they are 'for infant baptism' or 'practice infant baptism'. In seminary or theology writing, 'paedobaptist' is the standard label for the position, usually set against 'Baptist' or 'credobaptist'.

distinctions.note: Baptist usually refers to a denomination that baptizes only believers, so a paedobaptist is almost by definition not a Baptist in the usual sense.
A credobaptist baptizes only people who profess faith, which is the opposite position of a paedobaptist.
Anabaptist refers to a historical movement that rejected infant baptism, so it is the reverse of paedobaptist and should not be used as a synonym.

examples.professional: Our denomination is paedobaptist, so the new membership class explains how infant baptism connects to the covenant.
examples.analytical: Many paedobaptist writers argue that the household language in Acts assumes the presence of children within the covenant community.

nuance.analogy: A paedobaptist is like a parent who signs a child up for a family membership on the child's behalf, expecting the child to take up the membership later.
nuance.etymology: From 'paedobaptism', combining Greek 'pais, paidos' (child) with 'baptism'.
common_mistakes: Using 'paedobaptist' as an adjective in everyday speech when 'infant baptism' would sound more natural.
Confusing 'paedobaptist' with 'Anabaptist', which refers to a different group with opposite views.
nuance.biblical_note: The term is a modern theological label rather than a biblical word, but it rests on texts such as Acts 16:33, where a jailer is baptized with his household, and Colossians 2:11-12, which links baptism to circumcision. Supporters argue these passages show children included in the covenant community, while opponents argue they describe believing adults.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church baptizes infants and sees the practice as part of full initiation, along with chrismation and communion.
The Catholic Church baptizes infants as the sacrament that washes away original sin and makes the child a member of the Church.
Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches are paedobaptist, while Baptist, many Pentecostal, and Anabaptist-descended churches baptize only believers.

senses.definition: One of the many pieces of paper bound together within a book or similar document.
senses.example: The book which he was reading had 213 pages.

senses.definition: One side of a paper leaf in a bound document.
A collective memory; noteworthy event; memorable episode.
senses.example: a page from history

senses.definition: The type set up for printing a page.
senses.example: The typesetter locked the finished page into the chase before the press started rolling.

senses.definition: A screenful of text and possibly other content; especially, the digital simulation of one side of a paper leaf.
senses.example: Swipe to the next page to finish reading the chapter on your e-reader.

senses.definition: A web page.
senses.example: Her company's homepage loads quickly, but the product page takes almost ten seconds.

senses.definition: A block of contiguous memory of a fixed length.
senses.example: The operating system loaded the entire page into RAM before the program could run.

senses.definition: Clipping of memory page.
senses.example: The kernel swapped the least recently used page out to disk to free up memory.

senses.definition: A boy or girl employed to wait upon the members of a legislative body.
senses.example: As a page in the state senate, he carried messages between the chamber and the clerk's office.

senses.definition: An employee whose main purpose is to replace materials that have either been checked out or otherwise moved, back to their shelves.
senses.example: During summer break, she worked as a page at the public library, reshelving returned books.

senses.definition: A contrivance, such as a band, pin, snap, or the like, to hold the skirt of a woman’s dress from the ground.
senses.example: Before the dance, she fastened a page to her skirt so the hem would stay off the floor.

senses.definition: A track along which pallets carrying newly molded bricks are conveyed to the hack.
senses.example: The newly molded bricks rolled along the page toward the hack, drying in the sun.

senses.definition: Any one of several species of colorful South American moths of the genus Urania.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: (historical) A serving boy; a youth attending a person of high degree, especially at courts, often as a position of honor and education.
senses.example: The young page knelt before the king and carried his message across the hall.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (dated) A message sent to someone's pager.
senses.example: Hey, I left you a page an hour ago, so call me when you can.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To mark or number the pages of, as a book or manuscript.
senses.example: The editor paged the manuscript by hand, numbering each sheet before sending it to the printer.

senses.definition: To turn several pages of a publication.
senses.example: The patient paged through magazines while he waited for the doctor.

senses.definition: To furnish with folios.
senses.example: Before binding, the printer paged every ledger so the accountants could cross-reference entries.

senses.definition: To attend (someone) as a page.
senses.example: The young noble was sent to page the bishop during the long procession through the cathedral.

senses.definition: To call or summon (someone).
senses.example: Could you page the nurse to room twelve? Mr. Lopez needs help with his IV.

senses.definition: To call (somebody) using a public address system to find them.
senses.example: An SUV parked me in. Could you please page its owner?

senses.definition: (dated) To contact (someone) by means of a pager or other mobile device.
senses.example: I'll be out all day, so page me if you need me.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: One side of a sheet of paper in a book, magazine, or document, numbered and printed or written on.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single stressed syllable with a long 'ay' and a voiced 'j' sound at the end. Don't pronounce the g as a hard 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday word for a part of a document.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'page' for one side of a printed sheet, for the sheets of a book, and for web pages on a website. When referring to a location, they say 'turn to page 12' or 'on page 5'. A common idiom is 'on the same page', meaning in agreement, which Americans use often in meetings.

distinctions.note: A leaf is a whole sheet of paper with a page printed on each side, while a page is only one side of that sheet.
A sheet is a piece of paper in general, while a page is a specific printed or written side of a document.
A folio is a page number or a large-format sheet in a book, and it is more technical than the everyday word page.

examples.everyday: Can you turn to page twelve? I want to show you the recipe my mom wrote.
examples.professional: Please send the revised proposal, and make sure the summary is on the first page.
examples.analytical: The author's argument depends on the change of tone on the final page, which signals a shift from description to judgment.

nuance.analogy: A page is like one side of a single coin: a book is made of many sheets, and each sheet has two pages, front and back.
