nuance.etymology: From Latin 'pagina', meaning a side of a leaf or column of writing.
common_mistakes: Saying 'turned to the page' instead of 'turned to page' when naming a number.
Using 'page' for a whole sheet of paper, when Americans would say 'sheet' or 'leaf'.

page.etymology: Middle French *page*, from Latin *pagina*, from Proto-Indo-European **peh₂ǵ-*.

senses.definition: A Hesychast, an intellectual leader of the Hesychasts.
senses.example: Our church history class studied the Palamite leaders who defended hesychast prayer in fourteenth-century Byzantium.

senses.definition: Hesychastic.
senses.example: The Palamite tradition emphasizes stillness and the inner repetition of the Jesus Prayer.

core.definition: A follower of Gregory Palamas, a 14th-century Byzantine monk and theologian who defended hesychast prayer and the distinction between God's essence and energies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'light'. Non-native speakers often add an extra syllable or stress the second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized historical and theological term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in academic writing on Byzantine theology, Orthodox mysticism, or church history. In American seminaries and graduate courses you might hear it in lectures on hesychasm. Outside those settings it would puzzle most listeners, so explain it when you use it. The adjective is Palamite or Hesychastic depending on the emphasis of the discussion.

distinctions.note: A Hesychast is anyone who practices the contemplative prayer of stillness; a Palamite specifically defends Palamas's theology of that prayer and God's energies.
Barlaam of Calabria was Palamas's opponent in the 14th-century debate; a Barlaamite was on the other side of the controversy.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies Orthodox history said the Palamite debate is why some monks still talk about prayer as stillness.
examples.professional: In the seminar on Byzantine spirituality, the professor framed the reading list around the Palamite position on the energies of God.
examples.analytical: The Palamite distinction between God's unknowable essence and his communicable energies allowed the hesychast tradition to claim direct experience of God without violating divine transcendence.

nuance.analogy: Think of a Palamite as a defense attorney for a particular way of prayer: the case is about whether God can truly be encountered, not just known by reasoning.
nuance.etymology: Named after Gregory Palamas, the 14th-century Byzantine theologian, from Greek Palamas.
common_mistakes: Confusing Palamite with Hesychast, which is a broader term for the practice itself.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'puh-LAM-ite'.

traditions.view: Palamas is honored as a defender of the faith. His distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies is affirmed as a safeguard for real communion with God.
Catholic theology has generally upheld divine simplicity and has not accepted a real distinction between God's essence and energies. Palamas's teaching is therefore viewed with reservation.

Protestant traditions have rarely engaged Palamas's theology directly. Reformed thinkers generally affirm divine simplicity, while some Pietist and contemplative traditions show interest in the hesychast practice of prayer.

senses.definition: The act of feeling a part (or various parts) of a patient's body to detect (with the sense of touch) a state or condition of health, illness, or injury, such as the normality of organs or the presence or absence of tumors, swelling, muscle tension, etc.
senses.example: The nurse performed palpation of his abdomen to check for tenderness and swelling.

core.definition: The act of feeling parts of a patient's body with the hands to check for abnormalities such as swelling, tenderness or masses.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, PAY, with the final syllable reduced to shun. Keep the first syllable short, like pal in pal.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Palpation is standard in medical training, nursing and physical examinations in American clinics and hospitals. Patients usually hear the doctor say they will feel the area, so the word is mostly used by professionals and in medical writing. In everyday speech Americans would describe it as pressing or feeling the area.

distinctions.note: Palpation is an exam technique performed by a clinician, while palpitation is a symptom the patient feels in the heart.
Examination is the whole visit; palpation is one hands-on method within it.

examples.everyday: The nurse said palpation would show whether the swelling in my neck was just a cold.
examples.professional: Our clinical rubric scores students on accurate palpation and clear documentation of findings.
examples.analytical: Palpation reveals what the eye cannot, which is why diagnosis has long depended on the trained hand.

nuance.analogy: Palpation is like a tailor feeling fabric for hidden seams and thin spots before cutting.
nuance.etymology: From palpate, from Latin palpare, to touch softly.
common_mistakes: Confusing palpation with palpitation, the symptom of a racing heart.
Saying pal-PAY-shin with a sh-like vowel instead of the clear shun ending.

senses.definition: Having the properties of a panacea; solving everything.
senses.example: The consultant promised a panacean software fix that would solve every problem in our data pipeline.

core.definition: Able to cure everything or solve every problem; claimed to be a universal remedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, -SEE-, and make the final syllable a reduced 'un'. The word is related to panacea but has a different ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it usually criticizes an overly broad claim.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use panacean in ordinary speech; it appears mostly in essays, reviews or academic writing. Most people would say 'a cure-all' or 'a solution for everything.' If you use it, make sure your listener will understand the connection to panacea.

distinctions.note: Universal means applying to everything or everyone; panacean specifically suggests a cure or remedy for all problems.
Panacea is the noun for the remedy itself; panacean is the adjective describing its character.

examples.professional: The vendor's panacean pitch promised to fix every workflow problem with one tool.
examples.analytical: The essay critiques the panacean assumption that a single principle can resolve every moral dilemma.

nuance.analogy: Like a label that promises a cure for everything on the shelf.
nuance.etymology: Derived from panacea, from Greek panakeia, a universal remedy.
common_mistakes: Using panacean as a noun instead of an adjective.
Stressing the first syllable as PAN-uh-see-un.

senses.definition: Something or someone that appears powerful, strong or threatening but is in reality weak, ineffective, or unable to withstand challenge.
senses.example: The rival team looked fearsome on paper but turned out to be a paper tiger.

core.definition: A person, group, or thing that seems powerful or threatening but is actually weak and ineffective.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIE in tiger, and paper is lighter. The -er ending is a reduced, r-colored vowel, not a hard 'ghur'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dismissive. It mocks an opponent's apparent strength, and it can be used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use paper tiger in business, sports, and politics, often when a rival turned out to be less dangerous than feared. It sounds casual and is common in news commentary. A natural reply is 'Yeah, they talked big, but they folded fast.'

distinctions.note: A pushover is easily defeated or persuaded, while a paper tiger seemed formidable at first before its weakness appeared.
A bluff is a deliberate pretense of strength, while a paper tiger may be weak without intending to deceive.

collocations: turned out to be a paper tiger
dismiss him as a paper tiger
a paper tiger of a rival

examples.everyday: That guy at the gym talked big, but he turned out to be a paper tiger.
examples.professional: The competitor looked dangerous in the pitch deck, but it was a paper tiger once we saw its churn rate.
examples.analytical: Many nineteenth-century treaties were paper tigers, binding on paper but unenforceable when a signatory chose to ignore them.

nuance.analogy: Like a tiger costume made of paper: it looks fierce from a distance but tears at the first touch.
nuance.etymology: From Chinese zhǐ lǎohǔ, paper tiger, popularized in English by Mao Zedong's 1946 remarks.
common_mistakes: Using it for an animal or literal toy; the phrase is only figurative.
Stressing paper too strongly and making tiger sound flat.

paper-tiger.etymology: A Chinese, a phrase popularized by Mao Zedong, but of pre-modern origin.

senses.definition: To park a vehicle with side parallel to the curb or the side of the road in line with other parked vehicles.
senses.example: I still struggle to parallel park on busy streets downtown without hitting the curb.

core.definition: To park a car along the curb, lined up with the cars in front of and behind it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PARK, the second word, and 'parallel' keeps only a light stress on its first syllable. Keep the r in both words, and make the vowel in park the open 'ah' of American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly tense; it names a daily driving skill that many people find stressful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday driving talk and in driver's education; it is the usual term for backing into a curbside space between two cars. You might say 'Can you parallel park?' or 'I failed the parallel parking part of my driving test.' For other kinds of parking, Americans say 'pull in' or 'back in'.

distinctions.note: 'Back into' describes backing a car into a space, and may be head-first or angled; 'parallel park' means fitting the car along the curb.
Angle parking puts cars diagonally to the curb or the lane; parallel parking lines the car up along the curb.

collocations: parallel park on a busy street

examples.everyday: I can't parallel park in a tight spot, so I usually look for an open lot.
examples.professional: Can you parallel park the van near the loading dock? The curb there is short.
examples.analytical: Parallel parking is a useful test of spatial reasoning, since it requires coordinating steering, reversing and judging distance.

nuance.analogy: Like threading a needle with a car: small movements, careful timing, and a lot of reversing.
nuance.etymology: From parallel (adjective) and park (verb), from Old French parc, enclosure.
common_mistakes: Saying 'PAR-uh-lel park' with the wrong emphasis, so that 'park' sounds unstressed.
Using 'parallel parking' as a verb; the verb is 'parallel park', as in 'I parallel parked'.
Using a British-style 'park parallel' instead of the common American phrase.

senses.definition: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.
senses.example: drug paraphernalia

core.definition: Equipment, tools or accessories needed for a particular activity, often a large, miscellaneous collection of small items.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third-from-last syllable, NAY. Americans reduce the middle syllables heavily, so the -ia ending sounds like 'ee-uh' and the first syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest clutter or a lot of unnecessary stuff, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for gear or belongings, like camping paraphernalia, smoking paraphernalia, or a photographer's paraphernalia. It is often said with a slightly humorous or dismissive tone about a messy pile of things. For simple everyday items, 'stuff' or 'gear' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Equipment is specific and purposeful for a task; paraphernalia is a looser collection of accessories and related items.
Gear is the more casual American word for equipment, especially outdoors or sports; paraphernalia suggests a broader or more cluttered set.

examples.everyday: We need to pack all the camping paraphernalia into the back of the car before we leave.
examples.professional: Before the site visit, the engineering team collected all the testing paraphernalia and sensors from the lab.
examples.analytical: The ritual's paraphernalia, from incense to vestments, reveals how material objects mediate the sacred for the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a toolbox that holds everything from wrenches to rubber bands, paraphernalia is a mixed collection of gear.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin paraphernalia, from Greek parapherna, property beyond a dowry, from para (beside) and phernē (dowry).
common_mistakes: Saying 'a paraphernalia' as a countable noun; say 'a piece of equipment' or 'a set of paraphernalia' instead.
Mispronouncing the stress as PAIR-uh-fer-nay-lee-uh; the main stress is on NAY.

paraphernalia.etymology: Medieval Latin *paraphernālia* (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for *paraphernālia bona* (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of *paraphernālis*, from *parapherna* + *-ālis*, from Ancient Greek *παράφερνα*, a…

senses.definition: A package wrapped, as for shipment or transport.
senses.example: I saw a brown paper parcel on my doorstep.

senses.definition: An individual consignment of cargo for shipment, regardless of size and form.
senses.example: The shipping clerk weighed each parcel before loading it onto the freight truck.

senses.definition: An individual item appearing on an invoice or receipt (only in the phrase bill of parcels).
senses.example: The merchant's bill of parcels listed every item we had ordered last month.

senses.definition: A division of land bought and sold as a unit.
senses.example: I own a small parcel of land between the refinery and the fish cannery.

senses.definition: An indiscriminate or indefinite number, measure, or quantity; a collection; a group.
senses.example: A parcel of visitors arrived at the museum just as it was closing.

senses.definition: A small amount of food that has been wrapped up, for example a pastry.
senses.example: I bought a warm apple parcel from the bakery for the train ride.

senses.definition: A portion of anything taken separately; a fragment of a whole; a part.
senses.example: A certain piece of land is part and parcel of another piece.

senses.definition: To wrap something up into the form of a package.
senses.example: She parceled the leftover pot roast in foil and handed it to her son.

senses.definition: To wrap a strip around the end of a rope.
senses.example: Worm and parcel with the lay; turn and serve the other way.

senses.definition: To divide and distribute by parts or portions; often with off, out or into.
To add a parcel or item to; to itemize.
senses.example: Please parcel every charge onto the invoice so the client can see the breakdown.

core.definition: To divide something into portions and give them out, often with off or out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The verb has the same pronunciation as the noun, so the second syllable is a reduced 'l' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes dividing tasks, resources, or land.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parcel out most often for tasks, money, or responsibilities being distributed among people. The phrasal form is more natural than parcel alone. In a meeting, 'Let's parcel out the research tasks' sounds natural and organized.

distinctions.note: Divide is neutral and general; parcel out suggests distributing portions deliberately to several people.
Allocate is a formal business term; parcel out is more concrete and informal.

examples.everyday: Let's parcel out the chores so nobody ends up doing all the dishes.
examples.professional: I'll parcel out the testing work across the three teams so each owns a module.
examples.analytical: The Byzantine administration parceled out imperial land among loyal officials, binding their status to the state.

nuance.analogy: To parcel out is like dealing cards from a deck: each person gets a share, and the whole is divided among them.
nuance.etymology: From the noun parcel, from Old French parcelle, small part.
common_mistakes: Omitting out or off when the sense is distribution; say 'parcel out the work' rather than 'parcel the work.'
Confusing parcel with particle or partial, which are unrelated.

parcel.etymology: From Middle English *parcel*, from Old French *parcelle* (“a small piece or part, a parcel, a particle”), from Late Latin *particella*, diminutive of Latin *particula* (“particle”), diminutive of *pars* (“part, piece”).

senses.definition: Of, related to, or having characteristics of parody.
senses.example: The comedy sketch used a parodic tone, mocking the earnest speeches of televised political debates.

core.definition: Imitating a serious work or style in an exaggerated way, usually to mock it or make people laugh.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, RAH, not on the first. The first vowel is a weak schwa, and the r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it implies mockery or imitation, sometimes affectionate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parodic mostly in literary criticism, media studies and formal reviews to describe works that imitate a style in order to comment on it. In casual speech people say 'a spoof' or 'a parody'. Parodic can sound stiff in conversation, so use parody or spoof when speaking.

distinctions.note: Satirical focuses on criticizing vice or folly through wit, while parodic emphasizes imitating a specific work or style.
Comic describes anything funny; parodic specifically means imitating something in order to mock or amuse.

examples.everyday: That sketch was a parodic take on those cheesy cooking shows.
examples.professional: Our marketing team's parodic ad copies old car commercials to poke fun at our competitors' slogans.
examples.analytical: The novel's parodic structure imitates the Gothic romance only to expose its conventions.

nuance.analogy: A parodic work is like a funhouse mirror that copies a familiar face but exaggerates its quirks.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parōidia, parody, from para beside plus ōidē song.
common_mistakes: Using parodic as a noun; it is an adjective, so say a parodic style, not a parodic.
Confusing it with paradoxical; parodic means imitative and mocking, not contradictory.

senses.definition: To form a partnership; to decide to work together in a duo.
senses.example: After two years of solo work, the two developers decided to partner up on the startup.

core.definition: To pair with someone to work, play or do an activity together.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, and 'partner' keeps a lighter secondary stress. In fast speech the r links into the next word, so it sounds like 'part-ner-UP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a casual agreement to team up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use partner up in everyday talk, in schools, at the gym, on work projects and in group games. It is less formal than form a partnership. A natural reply is Sure, let's partner up or Sounds good, I'll partner with you.

distinctions.note: Team up is slightly broader and can mean joining a group; partner up usually means pairing with one person.
Pair off often means splitting a group into pairs; partner up is more about choosing a partner.
Collaborate is more formal and focuses on shared work; partner up is casual and about forming the pair.

examples.everyday: Want to partner up for trivia night on Thursday?
examples.professional: Let's partner up on the Q3 forecast so we don't duplicate work.
examples.analytical: Students who partner up on proofs often catch each other's logical errors before the final draft.

nuance.analogy: Partner up is like two people stepping onto the same dance floor: once they pair up, they move together.
nuance.etymology: Partner (from Middle English parcener, joint heir) with the adverbial particle up, indicating pairing off.
common_mistakes: Dropping up and saying partner with someone, which is correct but sounds less casual.
Adding to after up; the usual form is partner up with someone.

senses.definition: To celebrate at a party, to have fun, to enjoy oneself.
senses.example: We partied until the early hours.

senses.definition: To engage in flings, to have one-night stands, to sow one's wild oats.
senses.example: After his divorce, he started to party around town, dating a different person every week.

senses.definition: To take recreational drugs.
senses.example: Some students party on weekends and end up taking pills they never should.

senses.definition: To form a party (with).
senses.example: If you want to beat that monster, you should party with a healer.

senses.definition: A social gathering, usually of invited guests, which typically involves eating, drinking, and entertainment and often held to celebrate a particular occasion.
senses.example: I'm throwing a huge party for my 21st birthday.

senses.definition: A person or group of people constituting one side in a legal proceeding, such as in a legal action or a contract.
senses.example: The contract requires that the party of the first part pay the fee.

senses.definition: A political group considered as a formal whole, usually organized on a national basis, which contests elections and aims to form or take part in a government; a political party.
senses.example: The green party took 12% of the vote.

senses.definition: Active player characters organized into a single group.
senses.example: Our party of four adventurers entered the dungeon just after midnight.

senses.definition: A group of characters controlled by the player.
senses.example: My party includes a wizard, a rogue, and a healer for the campaign.

senses.definition: A group of people gathered together, especially temporarily, for a specific purpose such as travel or sport.
senses.example: We're expecting a large party from the London office.

senses.definition: A small group of birds or mammals.
senses.example: A party of quail scattered from the tall grass as we walked past.

senses.definition: (rare) A group of people forming one side in a given dispute, contest, etc. or united in maintaining a cause, policy, or opinion in opposition to others; a faction.
senses.example: The green party took 12% of the vote.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: With to: someone who takes part in an action or affair; an accessory.
senses.example: I can't possibly be (a) party to that kind of reckless behavior.

senses.definition: The Communist Party, especially as the sole political party of a communist state.
senses.example: She joined the Communist Party in her twenties and later wrote about her disillusionment.

senses.definition: A gathering of acquaintances so that one of them may offer items for sale to the rest of them.
senses.example: Tupperware party

senses.definition: A detachment of troops selected for a particular service or duty.
senses.example: boarding party

senses.definition: (dated) A person; an individual.
senses.example: He is a queer party.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated, rare) The feeling of solidarity with and support for one's political party; partisanship, especially in political matters.
senses.example: Party feeling ran so high in the 1880s that neighbors refused to speak across the aisle.
senses.label: dated, rare

senses.definition: (clarification of this definition is needed) Favoring one party; partisan.
senses.example: Her speech was too party to win over the undecided voters in the district.

senses.definition: Divided into parts of different tinctures, usually equal, and especially following the lines of one of the ordinaries.
senses.example: an escutcheon party per pale

senses.definition: (rare) Shared by two properties and serving to divide them.
senses.example: The contractor built a party wall that serves both houses and divides the two properties.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A social gathering, usually of invited guests, with food, drinks and entertainment, often held to celebrate an occasion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r clear. The final vowel is a light American 'ee', not a long 'ee' as in 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually suggests fun, friendship and celebration, though the political and legal senses are neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use party constantly for birthdays, holidays, housewarmings and casual get-togethers, and it is informal but polite. Saying 'Are you going to the party?' is natural. For a small, low-key gathering, Americans might say get-together or hangout, and for a formal event they might say reception or dinner.

distinctions.note: Gathering is a more general and neutral word for any group of people meeting; party implies food, drinks and fun.
Celebration focuses on marking an occasion; a party is the social event where that celebration happens.

examples.everyday: Do you want to come to my birthday party on Saturday?
examples.professional: We're planning a team party for the end of the quarter, so please send me your availability.
examples.analytical: A party in the older sense was a group of people who joined together for a common purpose, and the sense of social celebration developed later.

nuance.analogy: A party is like a pot that brings people together, with food, music and conversation filling it up.
nuance.etymology: From Old French partie, meaning a part or side, from Latin partita, meaning divided.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a party' instead of 'throw a party' or 'have a party'.
Using party for a formal event like a dinner speech, where Americans would say reception or dinner.

party.etymology: From Middle English *party*, *partye*, *partie*, from Anglo-Norman *partie*, from Old French *partie* (“side, part; portion, share; separation, division”), noun use of feminine of past participle of Old French *partir* (“to divide, separate”), from Latin…

conversation.text: Are you going to Jake's birthday party on Friday?
The party didn't really get going until after ten.
"How many in your party?" "Four, please."
Those guys love to party on the weekends.

senses.definition: Someone who attends a party or parties.
senses.example: Every partygoer at the rooftop gathering wore a bright paper crown and sang loudly.

core.definition: Someone who goes to parties, often frequently, whether or not they are the host or the most enthusiastic guest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PAR, with a clear r. The final -er is an unstressed American er sound, and goer rhymes with the verb go plus er, not with power.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a person's habits without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use partygoer in news reports, neighborhood talk, and everyday conversation to describe the people who attend a party or a series of parties. It is neutral, so it works well in polite speech. A natural reply might be Oh, you're a real partygoer, or Yeah, I'm usually at the back of the crowd.

distinctions.note: A guest has been invited to a particular party, while a partygoer is a general term for someone who regularly attends parties.
Party animal suggests enthusiasm and often excess, while partygoer is neutral and simply describes frequent attendance.

examples.everyday: Our neighbors are serious partygoers, so their backyard is full almost every weekend.
examples.professional: The event planner said most of the partygoers came from the sales team, so we changed the venue for next year.
examples.analytical: Sociologists have studied partygoers as a group, asking why some people seek out crowds while others keep to small gatherings.

nuance.analogy: Like a regular at a popular diner, you are known by sight to the staff and always show up when the place is busy.
nuance.etymology: Party comes from Old French partie; goer comes from the verb go, from Old English gan.
common_mistakes: Confusing partygoer with guest, when a guest is someone invited to a specific party.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound like a verb phrase rather than the common noun.

senses.definition: Jesus Christ symbolized as a sacrifice for the sins of humankind.
A lamb depicted with nimbus and bearing a flag (usually St. George's cross: argent a cross gules).
senses.example: The stained-glass window showed the Paschal Lamb with a halo and a red-cross banner.

senses.definition: (historical) The lamb eaten at Passover.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Jesus Christ, seen as the sacrificial lamb whose death fulfills the Passover; also the lamb eaten at the Jewish Passover.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PAS in paschal and LAM in lamb, since the adjective-noun phrase puts stress on the noun. Pronounce paschal as pass-kuhl, not pash-ul, and do not say the b in lamb.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and theological. It is a serious religious term, so it fits sermons, Bible study, and academic writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Paschal Lamb mainly in church, theological, and academic settings. In everyday conversation, most people say Lamb of God or simply the Passover lamb. A natural reply in a Bible study might be Yes, that connects Exodus to the cross, or I'd like to read that passage again.

distinctions.note: Lamb of God is the common Christian title for Jesus, while Paschal Lamb highlights his connection to the Passover sacrifice.
Passover lamb refers to the literal animal eaten at the Jewish feast, while Paschal Lamb usually refers to Christ or Christian imagery.
A scapegoat is a figure who carries away the guilt of others and is sent off, while the Paschal Lamb is a sacrifice that brings deliverance.

examples.everyday: Our pastor said Jesus is called the Paschal Lamb because he died around the time of Passover.
examples.professional: For the Bible study outline, I cited 1 Corinthians 5:7 to explain the Paschal Lamb imagery in the Gospel of John.
examples.analytical: The image of the Paschal Lamb links Christ's death to the Exodus sacrifice, and it frames the Eucharist as a meal rooted in Passover.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that opens a door in one story and unlocks the meaning of a later one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin paschalis, of Passover, from Greek paschalis, from pascha, Passover.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing paschal with a sh sound instead of the hard k of pass-kuhl.
Using Paschal Lamb as a casual term for any lamb dish, when it is a religious title.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew background is pesah, Passover, and the lamb is seh, the sheep or goat taken for the Passover sacrifice. In Exodus 12:3 to 7, Israel is told to take a lamb without blemish and mark the doorposts with its blood as a sign of protection. In John 1:29, John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and in 1 Corinthians 5:7, Paul names Christ as the Paschal Lamb who has been sacrificed.

traditions.view: Orthodox worship sings of Christ as the Paschal Lamb, especially at Pascha, and the image is central to the church's hymns and Eucharistic life.
Catholics connect the Paschal Lamb to the Mass, where Christ's sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist; the Agnus Dei prayer also invokes the Lamb of God.
Protestants generally read the image as a sign of Christ's once-for-all atoning death, while Lutheran and Reformed churches differ in how they describe Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper.

senses.definition: Pertaining to descent through male lines.

core.definition: Relating to descent or inheritance traced through the father's male line, so children belong to their father's family and clan.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LIN, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The final -al is a reduced 'ul,' so avoid saying 'pat-ri-LYNE-ee-al.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term used in anthropology, genealogy and law without any positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in anthropology, sociology, genealogy and religious studies, and in discussions of inheritance law. In casual talk people usually say 'on the father's side' instead. It is a neutral description, but it can sound academic or stiff at a dinner table.

distinctions.note: Matrilineal traces descent through the mother's line, so it is the direct opposite of patrilineal.
Bilateral descent counts both the mother's and father's lines equally, while patrilineal counts only the father's line.

examples.everyday: In our family the surname passes down the father's side, so I guess we are sort of patrilineal.
examples.professional: The genealogy database follows patrilineal descent, so records link each child to the father's surname and family line.
examples.analytical: Many ancient Near Eastern societies reckoned inheritance patrilineally, which shaped who could hold land and claim a family's title.

nuance.analogy: A patrilineal family tree is like a river that flows from one source, the father's line, down through each generation.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pater (father) and linea (line), with the English suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'patrilineal' with 'matrilineal,' which is the opposite.
Misplacing the stress as 'pat-ri-LYNE-ee-al' instead of pat-rih-LIN-ee-ul.
nuance.biblical_note: Patrilineal reckoning shapes the Bible's family records. Numbers 1:2 counts Israel by clans and fathers' houses, and Matthew 1:1-16 and Luke 3:23-38 trace Jesus through Joseph's male line. The Hebrew phrase bet 'av, 'house of the father,' names the family unit of such descent.

senses.definition: The act of providing approval and support; backing; championship.
senses.example: His vigorous patronage of the conservatives got him in trouble with progressives.

senses.definition: Customers collectively; clientele; business.
senses.example: The restaurant had an upper-class patronage.

senses.definition: The act or state of being a customer of some business.
senses.example: The restaurant had "Thank you for your patronage!" printed on its take-out bags.

senses.definition: A communication that indicates lack of respect by patronizing the recipient; condescension; disdain.
senses.example: Her email's patronage about my code review was more insulting than any criticism.

senses.definition: Granting favours or giving contracts or making appointments to office in return for political support.
senses.example: The mayor's office ran on patronage, handing out city jobs to loyal party workers.

senses.definition: Guardianship, as of a saint; tutelary care.
senses.example: Many farmers prayed for the patronage of Saint Isidore during the drought.

senses.definition: The right of nomination to political office.
senses.example: The family held the patronage of the parish, so they chose its priest.

senses.definition: Patronizing speech or behavior.
senses.example: He answered my question with a tone of patronage that made me want to leave.

senses.definition: To support by being a patron of.
senses.example: Wealthy families once patronaged the painters who worked in their Florence palazzos.

senses.definition: To be a regular customer or client of; to patronize.
senses.example: We have patronaged the same diner for years, and the waitress knows our order.

core.definition: Financial or public support given to a person, group, or cause, or the business that regular customers give to a shop or restaurant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with the sound of 'ij' as in 'ridge', not 'ahj'. The middle syllable is reduced and quick, and the r stays clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means support for a worthy cause, neutral for customers, but negative when it means favors such as political jobs handed out to allies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use patronage for government jobs or contracts given as favors, which is usually criticized. In the arts or charity, it sounds respectful. For ordinary businesses, people usually say 'business' or 'customers,' but 'thank you for your patronage' is a common, polite phrase on signs and in emails.

distinctions.note: Support is the general word for help of any kind; patronage implies a special relationship in which a patron gives money, status, or repeated business.
Sponsorship is usually a business arrangement tied to a named event or team; patronage is more personal, long-term, and often cultural or charitable.
Business is the everyday word for a company's customers; patronage is more formal and is mostly used for loyal relationships or polite thank-you messages.

examples.everyday: The little diner has stayed open for decades because of the loyal patronage of the neighborhood.
examples.professional: Thank you for your continued patronage, and please let me know if I can help with your next order.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the state's patronage of the sciences was a genuine commitment to knowledge or a means of securing political loyalty.

nuance.analogy: Patronage is like a greenhouse: it keeps a fragile plant alive and growing when the open weather would not.
nuance.etymology: From Latin patronus, 'protector,' through Old French patron; the suffix -age marks a condition or system.
common_mistakes: Confusing patronage with patronize; patronizing means condescending, not supporting.
Using 'patronage' for ordinary shoppers in casual speech; say 'customers' instead.

patronage.etymology: From Middle English *patronage*, from Old French *patronage*.

senses.definition: A pearl diver.
A boat used in pearl fishing.
A machine for pearling grain.
senses.example: The mill operator adjusted the pearler so the barley would come out smooth and white.

core.definition: A person who dives for or fishes for pearls, or a boat used in pearl fishing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PURL. The second syllable is a reduced 'er', like the end of 'water', not a full 'ler' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a historical or occupational term for pearl divers and their boats.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pearler in daily speech; they say pearl diver or pearl fisher. The word appears in historical writing, museum displays and fishing history, especially about Australia and the Pacific pearl industry.

distinctions.note: Pearl diver is the more common modern phrase; pearler is older and more technical.
A fisherman catches many kinds of fish; a pearler works specifically for pearls.

examples.everyday: My great-uncle worked as a pearler off the coast of Western Australia years ago.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit includes tools and photographs from the pearlers who worked the reef.
examples.analytical: Historians of colonial trade have studied how pearlers depended on Indigenous and Asian divers.

nuance.analogy: Like a diver who searches the ocean floor for hidden treasure.
nuance.etymology: From pearl with the agent suffix -er, meaning one who works with pearls.
common_mistakes: Saying 'PEAR-ler' like the fruit; the vowel is the 'er' sound of pearl.
Using pearler in modern speech when pearl diver is more natural.

senses.definition: A theory of the atonement holding that Christ, in his death, took on himself the punishment due to sinners, satisfying God's justice in their place.

core.definition: The view of the atonement that Christ died in sinners' place, bearing the punishment their sins deserved and so satisfying God's justice.

pronunciation.tip: Penal is PEE-nul, like 'penalty' without its short 'e'. In substitution, stress TOO; Americans say 'too', not 'tyoo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a label; for many evangelicals it is the heart of the gospel, while critics see it as too legal or violent.
nuance.usage_note: This is a common term in American evangelical theology, seminary courses and debates about the cross. It is often shortened to 'PSA' (penal substitutionary atonement). It is one of several 'atonement theories' along with Christus Victor, satisfaction and moral influence, and many theologians hold more than one together.

distinctions.note: Anselm's satisfaction theory says Christ restored the honor due to God; penal substitution, developed by the Reformers, says Christ bore the penalty for sin.
Christus Victor stresses Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil; penal substitution stresses his bearing judgment in our place.
The moral influence view says the cross changes us by showing God's love, rather than dealing with a debt or penalty.

examples.everyday: Our small group got into a long talk about penal substitution after the pastor said Jesus took our punishment.
examples.professional: The systematic theology course devotes two weeks to penal substitution and its critics.
examples.analytical: Penal substitution assumes that forgiveness without justice would compromise God's holiness, an assumption its critics challenge.

nuance.etymology: Penal from Latin poena 'penalty, punishment'; substitution from Latin substituere 'to put in place of'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing penal as 'PEN-ul'; say PEE-nul.
nuance.biblical_note: Supporters cite Isaiah 53:5-6, where the servant is wounded for our transgressions and the Lord lays on him the iniquity of us all; 2 Corinthians 5:21, where God made him to be sin who knew no sin; Galatians 3:13, where Christ became a curse for us; and 1 Peter 2:24, where he bore our sins in his body on the tree. In Romans 3:25 the RSV translates the key Greek word hilasterion as 'expiation', where some other versions say 'propitiation', a difference at the center of this debate.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology generally does not frame the cross in terms of the Father punishing the Son. It speaks of Christ trampling down death by death, healing human nature and opening the way to theosis, and many Orthodox writers criticize penal substitution as a Western legal framework.

Catholic teaching describes Christ's death as a sacrifice of atonement and as satisfaction for sin, drawing on Anselm and Aquinas, but it does not teach that the Father punished the Son. It stresses Christ's loving obedience offered on our behalf.

Penal substitution is central for Reformed and most evangelical Protestants and is taught by many Lutherans and Anglicans. Some Anabaptist, Wesleyan and mainline Protestants criticize it or place it beside other views such as Christus Victor.

senses.definition: A body suspended from a fixed support so that it swings freely back and forth under the influence of gravity, commonly used to regulate various devices such as clocks.
senses.example: The pendulum of the grandfather clock swung steadily, marking each second with a soft tick.

senses.definition: The tendency of a situation to oscillate (between two extremes).
senses.example: Public opinion has swung like a pendulum between fierce optimism and deep despair over the past decade.

senses.definition: A lamp, etc. suspended from a ceiling.
senses.example: A brass pendulum lamp hung above the dining table, casting warm light across the wooden floor.

senses.definition: A watch's guard-ring by which it is attached to a chain.
senses.example: Her grandfather's pocket watch dangled from a silver chain attached to a pendulum ring.

core.definition: A weight hung from a fixed point so it swings back and forth under gravity, used to keep time in clocks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle to a short uh. The final -um is a weak uhm, not the sound of loom. The j is like judge.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in clocks and physics. Figuratively it is neutral to negative, depending on whether the swing is seen as unstable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pendulum for the literal swinging weight in a grandfather clock or a science class demo. Figuratively, they say the pendulum has swung back, meaning public opinion or policy has moved to the opposite extreme, a phrase common in politics and news. In everyday talk, 'the pendulum has swung back' is natural. Pendulum is not used for a person's motion.

distinctions.note: Pendulum is the swinging object or motion; pendulous is an adjective meaning hanging heavily, and it does not describe swinging.
Swing is a general word for back-and-forth motion; pendulum is the specific device or a figurative shift between extremes.
Oscillation is the technical term for repeated back-and-forth change in physics or signals; pendulum is the concrete everyday example.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's clock has a brass pendulum that you can hear all over the house at night.
examples.professional: Our hiring policy has swung like a pendulum, from strict approvals to almost none, so we need steadier rules.
examples.analytical: Historians describe a pendulum of reform and reaction, in which each era's excesses provoke a correction that overshoots in the opposite direction.

nuance.analogy: The pendulum is like a metronome of history: it keeps swinging, and every extreme eventually sends it back toward the middle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pendulus 'hanging', from pendere 'to hang'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, saying PEN-doo-lum.
Using pendulum for a person who sways, or for any shift that is not a swing between two extremes.

pendulum.etymology: Borrowed from the neuter of Latin *pendulus* (“hanging”).

senses.definition: Careful with small amounts of money or over small matters.

core.definition: Careful about small sums of money while wasteful with larger ones, showing poor judgment about spending.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEN; the final -wise rhymes with 'eyes' and is pronounced 'wize', not 'wiss'. The second syllable is light.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes short-sighted judgment about money.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use pennywise in the saying 'penny-wise and pound-foolish,' meaning someone saves tiny amounts while wasting large ones, such as skipping car maintenance to save ten dollars. The adjective alone is rare. The saying is a mild criticism and is often said with humor among friends or colleagues.

distinctions.note: Penny-pinching describes stinginess in general; pennywise describes poor judgment, saving small amounts while losing more.
Thrifty is a positive word for wise spending; pennywise criticizes careless priorities.

examples.everyday: I skipped the oil change to save twenty bucks, which was penny-wise and pound-foolish when the engine failed.
examples.professional: Cutting the training budget was penny-wise, because the turnover that followed cost us far more.
examples.analytical: The policy is penny-wise and pound-foolish, saving small sums now at the cost of much larger public expenses later.

nuance.etymology: From penny plus wise; the full saying 'penny wise and pound foolish' is centuries old in English.
common_mistakes: Writing the adjective without a hyphen in the idiom; standard usage is penny-wise and pound-foolish.
Treating it as a simple synonym for cheap; it specifically means short-sighted about money.

senses.definition: Miserly; excessively cheap.
senses.example: The old man died a penurious wretch; eighty-thousand dollars in the mattress and as many holes in the roof.

senses.definition: Not bountiful; thin; scant.
senses.example: The penurious stew would have been more accurately labeled broth.

senses.definition: Impoverished; wanting for money.
senses.example: The poor penurious horde, naught in the cooking pot and naught in the belly.

core.definition: Extremely stingy with money, or very poor and short of money.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NYOOR, the second syllable. The yoo sound is one syllable in American English, and the ending is -ee-us, not -ee-ous.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies meanness or deprivation, so it can be harsh when describing a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use penurious in casual speech. In conversation they say stingy, cheap or tight-fisted. Penurious sounds formal or literary, and it often appears in fiction, editorials and formal writing about poverty or meanness.

distinctions.note: Stingy is common and informal, describing a reluctance to spend; penurious is formal and can also describe actual poverty.
Frugal is positive and means careful with money; penurious is negative and suggests meanness or deprivation.

examples.everyday: My uncle is so penurious that he reuses the same tea bag twice.
examples.professional: The penurious budget left the team no room for testing or training.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays the penurious household as a moral system in which every coin is weighed against dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like a wallet that refuses to open even when the price is fair.
nuance.etymology: From Latin penuria (want, need), with the English suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Using penurious as a casual word for cheap in everyday talk, where stingy sounds more natural.
Pronouncing it with three syllables (pen-yoo-ri-us) instead of puh-NYOOR-ee-us.

senses.definition: In a permissible manner.

core.definition: In a way that is allowed or acceptable under the rules, law or a moral standard.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MIS, the second syllable of permit-related words. The -ibly ending reduces to a quick 'uh-blee', so do not pronounce each letter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes whether something is allowed, without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Permissibly is a formal word used in legal, technical and philosophical writing, such as a contract or policy document. In everyday speech, Americans say 'you're allowed to' or 'it's okay to'. Use it when you want to emphasize that something falls within the rules.

distinctions.note: Permissibly means within the rules, while permissively means in a lenient or tolerant way.
Legally refers specifically to law, while permissibly covers any rule, policy or ethical standard.

examples.everyday: The sign says we can permissibly bring our own snacks to the game, so the cooler is fine.
examples.professional: The contractor may permissibly subcontract the wiring work if the client approves it in writing.
examples.analytical: An act may be permissibly performed under one moral theory and impermissible under another, so the verdict depends on the framework.

nuance.analogy: Acting permissibly is like walking on the marked path in a park: you are free to move, as long as you stay within the boundaries.
nuance.etymology: From permissible, with the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using permissibly where the meaning is 'permissively' (tolerantly), which changes the sense.
Stressing the first syllable instead of MIS.

senses.definition: A general belief that bad things will happen.
senses.example: Her pessimism about the project's timeline turned out to be justified when two vendors missed deadlines.

senses.definition: The doctrine that this world is the worst of all possible worlds.
senses.example: Leibniz's optimism stood in sharp contrast to the pessimism of later philosophers who saw the world as hopelessly corrupt.

senses.definition: The condition of being pessimal.

core.definition: The tendency to expect bad outcomes and to see the worst side of situations or people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PES. The last syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like zum, not zam or zim.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a gloomy outlook and can sound like criticism if you say someone has it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pessimism in everyday conversation and at work, often about the economy, a project, or a sports team. Calling someone a pessimist can sound judgmental, so people often say they are being realistic. The opposite is optimism, and you can name the mood in a friendly way.

distinctions.note: Cynicism is a distrust of people's motives; pessimism is an expectation that things will go badly.
Realism is an honest view of how things are; pessimism is a more negative expectation that may go beyond the evidence.

examples.everyday: I can't shake this pessimism about the weather; I'm sure it's going to rain on our picnic.
examples.professional: There's some pessimism on the team about the launch date, but the testing numbers look good.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's pessimism rests on the claim that suffering outweighs any good in human life.

nuance.analogy: Pessimism is like wearing gray-tinted glasses: everything still looks the same, but it all seems darker.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pessimus, the worst, with the suffix -ism, coined in the 1700s as the opposite of optimism.
common_mistakes: Using pessimism to mean realism when you only mean caution.
Saying pessimist as an adjective instead of pessimistic.

senses.definition: Someone who habitually expects the worst outcome; one who looks on the dark side of things.

core.definition: A person who habitually expects things to turn out badly and focuses on the negative side of situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ist is a short, unstressed syllable. Don't say 'pess-ih-MIST' or stretch the middle vowels; the second syllable is a quick 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a pessimist is a mild criticism implying they are gloomy or unhelpfully doubtful. Some people describe themselves as realists instead, which sounds more positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in everyday conversation, at work and in the news, often to describe a person's outlook or a commentator's tone. You can say 'I'm not a pessimist, I'm just realistic' to soften it. Saying 'You're such a pessimist' to a friend is common and usually friendly teasing, but it can sting if said in a serious argument.

distinctions.note: A cynic doubts that people are sincere or good, while a pessimist expects bad outcomes.
A realist accepts facts as they are without expecting the worst, whereas a pessimist leans toward gloom.

examples.everyday: Don't be such a pessimist; the game isn't over yet.
examples.professional: Our project manager is a pessimist about the launch date, so she always builds in an extra week.
examples.analytical: Critics often label the philosopher a pessimist, yet his arguments about suffering are more carefully reasoned than that label suggests.

nuance.analogy: A pessimist is like a weather forecaster who only predicts storms, even on sunny days.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pessimus, meaning worst, the superlative of malus, meaning bad.
common_mistakes: Using 'pessimist' as an adjective; the adjective is 'pessimistic', as in 'a pessimistic view'.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'pes-SIM-ist' instead of 'PES-ih-mist'.

senses.definition: A voltmeter that uses the potential at a glass electrode to determine the pH of the solution in which it is immersed.
senses.example: The lab technician calibrated the pH meter with buffer solutions before testing the soil samples.

core.definition: An electronic instrument that measures how acidic or basic a liquid is, using a glass electrode placed in the solution.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters P and H, with the stress on the second letter's sound 'aych.' Then stress MEE in 'meter,' and reduce the final syllable to a quick 'ter.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term used in labs, farms, and water treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'pH meter' in science classes, labs, aquarium hobbies, brewing, and agriculture. A cheaper handheld device is often called a 'pH tester,' and paper strips that change color are 'pH strips' or 'test strips.' In casual talk, people may simply say 'the pH' when discussing a reading.

distinctions.note: Litmus paper changes color to show only whether a liquid is acid or base, while a pH meter gives a numerical reading.
A conductivity meter measures how well a solution carries electricity, which relates to dissolved ions, not directly to acidity.

examples.everyday: My sourdough starter is acting strange, so I'm borrowing a friend's pH meter to check it.
examples.professional: The water treatment plant logs pH meter readings every hour to keep its discharge within permit limits.
examples.analytical: A pH meter responds to hydrogen ion activity rather than concentration, so readings in concentrated solutions can mislead without correction.

nuance.analogy: A thermometer for acidity: it turns a hidden chemical quality into a number you can read.
nuance.etymology: Short for power of hydrogen; the 'p' comes from German Potenz (power) and 'H' is the symbol for hydrogen, a term introduced by Søren Sørensen in 1909.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pH' as one word, like 'pee' or 'pah': pronounce the letters, pee-aych.
Using 'pH meter' and 'pH tester' interchangeably for all devices: the meter usually refers to an electronic instrument with a probe.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a pharaoh.
Impressively large or luxurious.
senses.example: The senator's pharaonic mansion had marble floors, a private cinema, and an indoor lake.

senses.definition: Tyrannical or brutally oppressive.
senses.example: Under the pharaonic rule of the regional governor, villagers lived in constant fear of arrest.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to infibulation as a means of female genital mutilation.
senses.example: Human rights workers documented pharaonic circumcision practices in several communities, a procedure involving infibulation.

core.definition: Huge, lavish or grand in scale, like something built for an ancient Egyptian pharaoh; or relating to a pharaoh.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, -AH-, which is a short, open 'ah' sound. Many learners stress the first syllable or say 'fair-OH-nik' by mistake.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative or ironic when used for projects, budgets or buildings that are excessively grand; neutral when describing ancient Egyptian history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news, business writing and commentary to criticize something that is wildly expensive or overblown, such as a 'pharaonic project' or a 'pharaonic budget'. It is not an everyday word, so you will mainly see it in writing and formal argument. When talking about ancient Egypt, Americans simply say 'Egyptian' or 'of the pharaohs'.

distinctions.note: Monumental means very large or significant in general; pharaonic adds the idea of extravagance, royal power or excess.
Lavish describes expensive, generous spending; pharaonic describes something that is vast in size and sometimes tyrannical in spirit.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's new backyard pool is so pharaonic that it has its own waterfall and a bar.
examples.professional: Leadership wants a pharaonic data platform that would cost three times the original budget, so we need a smaller pilot first.
examples.analytical: Critics of the stadium argue that its pharaonic scale reflects the city's ambitions more than the needs of its residents.

nuance.analogy: Like a huge monument built to show off power, something pharaonic is so big that it seems designed to outlast its own purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin pharao, from Greek pharaō, from Hebrew par'oh, from Egyptian per-aa, 'great house'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'fair-OH-nik' instead of 'fair-ay-AH-nik'.
Using 'pharaonic' to mean simply 'old' or 'ancient' rather than 'grand, lavish or excessive', or as a neutral term for anything Egyptian.

senses.definition: The humanistic study of texts and their languages, especially ancient or classical languages.
(rare) Love and study of learning and literature, broadly speaking.
senses.example: Her grandfather spent decades on philology, reading old manuscripts for the love of language and letters.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The historical study of written texts and the languages they were written in, especially ancient and classical languages.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LAH, the middle syllables are weak, and the final -gy is pronounced like the j in judge followed by ee. Do not stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals serious academic study and can sound lofty in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use philology mostly in university departments of classics, comparative literature and languages. For the modern scientific study of language, Americans usually say linguistics. The older broad sense of love of learning is rare and literary, so avoid it in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Linguistics describes language structure in any period, often with scientific methods; philology interprets texts and their historical and cultural context.
Textual criticism establishes the exact wording of a text from its manuscripts; philology is broader and includes interpreting the language and history behind it.

examples.everyday: I took a philology course in college, and it's the reason I still enjoy reading old English poems.
examples.professional: Our digital humanities group uses philology to check how the translations of the Psalms differ across the earliest editions.
examples.analytical: Philology attends to the language of a text as evidence of its historical setting, not only to the claims the text makes.

nuance.analogy: Philology is like forensic science for texts: it reads the small physical traces of language to reconstruct how a text was made and understood.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philologia, 'love of learning or words', from philos 'loving' and logos 'word, reason'.
common_mistakes: Using philology for modern language science; in American English, linguistics is the usual term.
Stressing the last syllable or saying fi-LOL-uh-jee; the stress falls on the first LAH in the second syllable.

philology.etymology: Middle English *Philologie*, from Latin *philologia*, from Ancient Greek *φιλολογίᾱ* (“love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

senses.definition: (dated) A piano.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The full historical name for the piano, an instrument whose keys make hammers strike strings to produce soft or loud notes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the AN syllable, as in piano. The last syllable forte is pronounced fort in English, not the Italian for-tay, and the r is clearly heard in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned; it can sound stiff or precious in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say piano. Pianoforte appears mainly in music history, older scores, and some formal concert titles, and it can sound dated or stiff in everyday talk. If you hear it, it is the same instrument, so you can simply answer with piano.

distinctions.note: Both name the same instrument; piano is the normal modern word, while pianoforte is older and more formal.
Fortepiano usually names the early instruments of the late eighteenth century, which have a lighter sound than modern pianos, while pianoforte is the general name.

examples.everyday: My grandmother still calls her old upright a pianoforte, which always makes me smile.
examples.professional: The printed score lists the piece for pianoforte and strings, so check the edition before the rehearsal.
examples.analytical: The shift from the harpsichord to the pianoforte in the late eighteenth century changed how composers thought about dynamics.

nuance.analogy: Calling a piano a pianoforte is like calling a smartphone a telephone: correct, but it sounds old-fashioned.
nuance.etymology: From Italian piano e forte, meaning soft and loud, describing the instrument's ability to play both.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing forte as the Italian for-tay instead of fort
Using pianoforte in casual speech where piano is expected

senses.definition: One who steals from the pocket of a passerby, usually by sleight of hand.
senses.example: A pickpocket bumped into me on the crowded subway and vanished.

senses.definition: To pick pockets; to steal.
senses.example: Tourists should keep their wallets zipped because thieves pickpocket crowds near the station.

core.definition: A thief who steals wallets, phones, or other valuables from people's pockets or bags, often in crowds.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, with a secondary stress on 'pock'. The 'pah' vowel matches 'cot' in American speech, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it refers to a criminal. It is often used as a warning in travel and public-transport contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pickpocket for a thief who steals in crowds, often at tourist sites, subways, or concerts. Warnings like 'Watch out for pickpockets' are common in travel advice. The word is informal enough for everyday talk, and the usual verb is 'to pick pockets'.

distinctions.note: Thief is the general word for anyone who steals; pickpocket specifically means someone who steals from people's pockets or bags.
A robber uses force or threats, while a pickpocket steals secretly, usually without the victim noticing.

collocations: a crowded area full of pickpockets

examples.everyday: Keep your wallet in your front pocket because there are pickpockets on this train.
examples.professional: Our security team sent a notice about pickpockets near the conference registration desk.
examples.analytical: The pickpocket depends on the victim's attention being directed elsewhere, which is why crowds offer such good cover.

nuance.analogy: A pickpocket is like a shadow that moves quietly through a crowd and takes something without being noticed.
nuance.etymology: From pick (to take) plus pocket.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'pock-it' with a long vowel; the American vowel is short and the last syllable is reduced.
Using steal alone in travel warnings; say 'pickpockets' or 'pick pockets' for the specific crime.

senses.definition: Made or done in pieces or one stage at a time.
senses.example: a piecemeal approach

senses.definition: Piece by piece; in small amounts, stages, or degrees.
senses.example: The city repaired the bridge piecemeal, closing one lane at a time for years.

senses.definition: Into pieces or parts.
senses.example: The old radio fell off the shelf and broke piecemeal across the tile floor.

senses.definition: To divide or distribute piecemeal; dismember.
senses.example: The buyer planned to piecemeal the failing company and sell each division separately.

senses.definition: A fragment; a scrap.
senses.example: Only a piecemeal of the ancient map survived the fire.

core.definition: Done in separate stages or small parts over time, rather than all at once and according to a clear plan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEES, not the second. The ending 'meal' sounds like the word 'meal' but is pronounced 'meel'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It often suggests a lack of overall planning or coordination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in business, policy, and news, such as 'a piecemeal approach to reform'. It is criticism when someone argues that a whole problem needs a comprehensive solution. In casual speech, people say 'bit by bit' or 'little by little' instead.

distinctions.note: Gradual describes slow change over time, which can be neutral or positive, while piecemeal suggests disconnected or poorly planned changes.
Incremental describes deliberate small steps toward a goal and is often positive in software and business, while piecemeal suggests a lack of overall design.
Fragmented describes something broken into disconnected parts, while piecemeal describes how something is done or added step by step.

examples.everyday: The landlord fixed the roof piecemeal, so every rainstorm brings a new leak.
examples.professional: Our team has been adding features piecemeal, which makes the release notes hard to follow.
examples.analytical: Piecemeal reform can succeed locally, but it often leaves contradictions that a comprehensive design would avoid.

nuance.analogy: Like patching a leaky boat one board at a time instead of rebuilding its hull.
nuance.etymology: From piece plus -meal, an old English suffix meaning 'portion' or 'measure'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the second syllable, saying 'pees-MEEL'.
Confusing it with 'piecework', which means work paid by the unit completed.

piecemeal.etymology: From Middle English *pecemele*, from *pece* (“piece”) + *mele* (from Old English *mǣlum* (“at a time”), dative plural form of *mǣl* (“time, measure”), taking the place of; equivalent to *piece* + *-meal*.

senses.definition: A soldier armed with a pike.
A person who operates a turnpike.
senses.example: The pikeman stepped out of his tollhouse and collected a penny from each rider.

senses.definition: A miner who works with a pick.
senses.example: The pikeman swung his heavy pick at the coal seam all morning long.

core.definition: A foot soldier armed with a pike, a long spear with a steel point, mainly in the 1500s and 1600s.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PIKE. The second syllable is reduced to 'muhn', not a full 'man'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pikeman in history classes, historical fiction, museum displays, and reenactment groups. In modern speech it would confuse people, so for a toll collector Americans say toll booth worker. Use it when discussing early modern armies.

distinctions.note: A musketeer carried a firearm; a pikeman carried a long spear.
A halberdier carried a halberd, a combined axe and spear; a pikeman carried a plain long pike.

examples.everyday: My kid's history project was about English pikemen from the 1500s.
examples.professional: For the museum exhibit, we need reproduction gear for the pikemen in the battle diorama.
examples.analytical: Historians credit pikemen with holding infantry lines, but muskets gradually made their formation obsolete.

nuance.analogy: A pikeman was the human fence of an early army, holding the line with length rather than speed.
nuance.etymology: From pike (a long spear) plus man.
common_mistakes: Using pikeman for a modern toll collector, which is not the usual American term.
Giving the second syllable a full vowel, as in 'pike-man'.

senses.definition: The plant, Arachis hypogaea, that bears peanuts.
senses.example: Grandpa planted pinders along the south fence every spring, and we roasted their nuts all winter.

core.definition: A regional Southern American word for a peanut, the nut-like seed pod of a leguminous plant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PINE, and end with a rhotic 'er' sound, like 'der' with the r colored. The vowel is a diphthong, so it sounds like 'pine' and not 'pin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and folksy. It sounds regional and old-fashioned outside the South.
nuance.usage_note: 'Pinder' is a rare, regional word for peanut that some Southern speakers still use. Most Americans say 'peanut', and that is the word to use in stores and restaurants. The older sense 'poundkeeper', one who impounds stray animals, is archaic and rarely used today.

distinctions.note: Peanut is the standard American word and is understood everywhere. Pinder is a regional term used mainly in parts of the South and may confuse people elsewhere.
A pound keeper is a current job title for someone who looks after impounded animals. Pinder in that sense is archaic and should not be used in modern conversation.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always kept a jar of salted pinders on the porch for visitors.
examples.professional: Our snack team buys pinders from Georgia growers, but in the product labels we always say peanuts.
examples.analytical: Regional words such as pinder show how vocabulary for everyday foods can persist in dialect long after standard English has moved on.

common_mistakes: Using 'pinder' in a national or business setting, where 'peanut' is expected.
Pronouncing it with a short 'i' like 'pin-der', instead of the diphthong in 'pine'.
Assuming it is a common standard word, when most Americans have never heard it.

pinder.etymology: Via from *mpinda* (“peanut”), also borrowed in Dutch as *pinda*.

senses.definition: Concise and meaningful.
Of, like, or abounding in pith; spongy or having small holes or pits.
senses.example: She gave a pithy summary of the report that fit neatly on a single index card.

core.definition: Expressing a lot in few words; concise, forceful and meaningful. Used of speech or writing that is brief but memorable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The th is voiceless, as in think, and the final -y is a light /i/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises speech or writing that is clear and well chosen.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pithy to praise a short, clever comment, a speech or a headline, such as 'a pithy summary' or 'a pithy quote.' It is a somewhat formal word, so it sounds natural in writing, teaching or media. A typical reply is 'That's pithy, I like it.'

distinctions.note: Brief only means short, while pithy means short and also meaningful or sharp.
Concise is neutral and technical, while pithy adds a sense of wit or memorable force.

examples.everyday: My dad always has a pithy comment about the weather.
examples.professional: Give me a pithy summary of the project status for the executive slide.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues its thesis in pithy sentences that reward slow, careful reading.

nuance.analogy: A pithy remark is like a well-cut gem: small, but clear and bright.
nuance.etymology: From pith, from Old English pitha, meaning the core or essence of something.
common_mistakes: Using pithy to mean small or short in size.
Confusing pithy with pitiful, which has a very different meaning.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being a plutocracy.

core.definition: Relating to a plutocracy, a society or government controlled by the wealthy, who hold most of the political power.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'KRAT', with a lighter stress on 'ploo'. Do not say 'PLOO-tuh-cratic' with the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes a system where money buys influence, so it is common in political argument and commentary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'plutocratic' in political journalism, history and debates about inequality, campaign finance or elite power. It sounds formal and somewhat academic, so in casual talk people more often say 'run by the rich'. Using it can signal a critical view of the system, so use it with care in a mixed group.

distinctions.note: 'Oligarchic' describes rule by a small group, which may not be wealthy, while 'plutocratic' specifically means that wealth is the basis of power.
'Aristocratic' refers to rule by a hereditary nobility or social elite, while 'plutocratic' refers to rule by those with money.

examples.everyday: My neighbor complains that the city council is basically run by plutocratic developers.
examples.professional: The report warns that our new funding model could entrench a plutocratic structure in which major donors set the agenda.
examples.analytical: Critics describe the modern campaign system as plutocratic, since fundraising capacity increasingly decides which candidates reach the ballot.

nuance.analogy: A plutocratic system is like a club where the membership fee is your bank balance, and the rules are written by those who can afford it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ploutokratia, from ploutos, 'wealth', and kratos, 'power' or 'rule'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'plutocratic' with 'democratic' or 'aristocratic', which describe different sources of power.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PLOO-tocratic', rather than the 'KRAT' syllable.

senses.definition: The spirit or soul.
One of three levels of a human being, the spirit, along with the body and soul.
senses.example: In his theology seminar, he explained how the pneuma, distinct from soul and body, animates the believer.

senses.definition: A neume.
senses.example: The monk pointed to the pneuma above the Latin text, marking the melody's rising line.

core.definition: In Christian theology, the Spirit or breath of God, or the spiritual life-giving principle in a human being.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'p' is silent, so start with the 'n' sound. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'a' is a reduced 'uh' sound, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pneuma outside theology, philosophy, and classics. In a church or Bible study you might hear it in a sermon or lecture, where it refers to the Greek word behind spirit or breath in the New Testament. In casual conversation, people say 'spirit' or 'breath' instead. Using it in everyday speech may sound overly academic.

distinctions.note: Psyche usually means the mind or personality in psychology, while pneuma refers to the breath or spirit as a divine or life-giving principle in theology.
Spirit is the everyday English word with a wide range of meanings, while pneuma is a technical term tied to the Greek of the New Testament and early Christian philosophy.

examples.everyday: In Bible study, our pastor said the Greek word pneuma can mean either breath or spirit.
examples.professional: For the seminar handout, I translated pneuma as spirit and noted that it also means breath in John 3.
examples.analytical: Paul's use of pneuma distinguishes the animating divine breath from the merely natural life of the body and soul.

nuance.analogy: Pneuma is like the wind that fills a sail: invisible, life-giving, and felt in its movement.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pneuma (breath, wind, spirit), from pneein (to breathe).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent initial 'p' as a separate sound.
Confusing pneuma with the more common English word spirit, which has broader everyday meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word pneuma means breath, wind, or spirit and is used throughout the New Testament for the Holy Spirit and for the spirit of a person. John 3:8 uses the same word for both wind and the Spirit, so the image of invisible movement is central. Romans 8:16 says the Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 lists spirit, soul, and body as parts of a person to be kept sound.

pneuma.etymology: From Ancient Greek *πνεῦμα* (“wind, breath, spirit”), from *πνέω* (“I blow, breathe”).

senses.definition: A person who trespasses in order to take game illegally, one who poaches; a person who illegally takes animals or plants from the wild.
senses.example: The park ranger caught a poacher hiding near the creek with an unlicensed rifle.

senses.definition: A vessel with shallow cuplike compartments in which eggs are cooked over boiling water.
senses.example: I bought a stainless steel poacher so my eggs would stay intact in simmering water.

senses.definition: An attacker with good movement inside the penalty box.
senses.example: The striker's quick instincts made him a dangerous poacher in the penalty box all season.

senses.definition: Any of type of fish in the family Agonidae, also known as alligatorfish, starsnout, hooknose and rockhead.
senses.example: Divers spotted a poacher resting on the sandy seabed, camouflaged among the rocks.

senses.definition: An American wigeon (Anas americana).
senses.example: Through the binoculars we spotted a poacher dabbling in the marsh at dawn.

core.definition: A person who illegally hunts or fishes on someone else's land or in protected areas, taking animals or plants from the wild.
