core.definition: A relaxed, drooping posture in which the head and shoulders hang forward, or a person who is lazy or slow to act.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first and only syllable, with a diphthong 'ow' like 'out'. Make the final 'ch' a firm sound, not a 'sh'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative; it suggests poor posture, lack of energy or lack of effort, though it can be neutral when describing relaxed sitting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slouch most often as a verb in everyday speech, as in 'Sit up, don't slouch'. As a noun, it describes a drooping posture or, informally, a lazy person, as in 'He's a real slouch at the office'. In formal contexts it is used with a little more care, and it is considered mildly rude when said directly to someone about their character.

distinctions.note: Posture is the neutral word for how a person holds their body, while slouch is a specific, usually poor posture.
Lean describes a deliberate tilt against something, while slouch describes a loose, drooping body position.

examples.everyday: Sit up straight, you've been slouching on the couch all afternoon.
examples.professional: Slouching in your chair during video calls can make you look less engaged than you are.
examples.analytical: The painter's figures slouch in ways that suggest weariness and resignation rather than physical fatigue alone.

nuance.analogy: A slouch is like a tent pole that has bent under its own weight, losing its structure and sagging toward the ground.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly related to a Middle English word for a sluggish or heavy person.
common_mistakes: Using slouch as a formal noun for posture without considering the negative connotation.
Pronouncing the 'ch' as a 'sh' sound.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being small.
senses.example: His smallness didn't bother him, except when he needed something off the top shelf.

senses.definition: The result or product of being small.

core.definition: The quality or state of being small in size, amount, or importance; a lack of largeness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SMAWL. The final -ness is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'nuhs'; do not add a full vowel after the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be negative when describing something disappointing, such as a small room, or positive when describing modesty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smallness mainly in formal writing and literary descriptions, such as the smallness of a town or a budget. In everyday speech they usually say the word small directly, as in I was surprised how small the room was. The noun works best when you want to make a size or scale into a topic.

distinctions.note: Size is the neutral measure of how big or small something is; smallness is more abstract and often carries a judgment about limitation or insignificance.
Littleness is an older, more emotional term and is rare in modern American English.
Modesty refers to humility or a lack of pride; smallness refers only to limited size, amount, or importance.

examples.everyday: I was surprised by the smallness of the apartment, but it was cozy once we unpacked.
examples.professional: Despite the smallness of the team, they shipped the release on schedule.
examples.analytical: The smallness of the sample makes it hard to draw firm conclusions about the effect.

nuance.analogy: Like a pocket watch: its smallness is part of what makes it impressive, though it can hide complex machinery.
nuance.etymology: From small (Old English smæl) plus the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of.
common_mistakes: Saying the smallness of the house is good when you mean it is cramped; the word can be neutral or negative, so add context.
Using smallness when you simply mean small in everyday speech; American speakers prefer the adjective small.

senses.definition: To make straightforward or easy.
senses.example: Clear instructions and a short checklist will smooth the onboarding process for new hires.

senses.definition: To make smooth or even.
senses.example: Sand the wood lightly to smooth the rough edges before you apply the stain.

senses.definition: To reduce to a particular shape or form by pressure; to press, to flatten.
senses.example: to smooth cloth with a smoothing iron

senses.definition: To calm or palliate.
senses.example: to smooth a person's temper

senses.definition: To capture important patterns in the data, while leaving out noise.
senses.example: Apply a rolling average to smooth the noisy sensor readings before fitting the model.

senses.definition: To stroke; especially to stroke an animal's fur.
senses.example: Can I smooth your cat?

senses.definition: Having a texture that lacks friction. Not rough.
Without difficulty, problems, or unexpected consequences or incidents.
senses.example: We hope for a smooth transition to the new system.

senses.definition: Bland; glib.
senses.example: His smooth answers during the hearing sounded rehearsed and never addressed the actual question.

senses.definition: Flowing or uttered without check, obstruction, or hesitation; not harsh; fluent.
senses.example: Her smooth delivery of the sermon made the hard passage from Romans sound effortless.

senses.definition: Suave; sophisticated.
senses.example: He wore a tailored suit and had a smooth manner that charmed every donor in the room.

senses.definition: Natural; unconstrained.
senses.example: Her smooth stride on the trail showed years of hiking without any strain.

senses.definition: Unbroken.
senses.example: The smooth line of hills rolled uninterrupted all the way to the horizon.

senses.definition: Placid, calm.
senses.example: The lake was smooth as glass that early morning, so we launched the kayaks.

senses.definition: Lacking projections or indentations; not serrated.
senses.example: Choose a knife with a smooth blade if you mostly slice soft tomatoes.

senses.definition: Not grainy; having an even texture.
Having a pleasantly rounded flavor; neither rough nor astringent.
senses.example: This Merlot has a smooth finish with no bitterness, which makes it easy to drink.

senses.definition: Having derivatives of all finite orders at all points within the function’s domain.
senses.example: The proof requires that the potential function be smooth on the entire open domain.

senses.definition: That factors completely into small prime numbers.
senses.example: The sieve searches for every smooth integer up to one billion in the factor base.

senses.definition: Lacking marked aspiration.
senses.example: Some Greek voiceless stops are smooth, while their rough counterparts carry a puff of breath.

senses.definition: Involuntary and non-striated.
senses.example: Smooth muscle lines the walls of the intestine and works without conscious control.

senses.definition: Smoothly.
senses.example: smooth-running, smooth-tongued, smooth-spoken

senses.definition: Something that is smooth, or that goes smoothly and easily.
senses.example: Sanding for an hour gave the tabletop a glassy smooth that felt perfect under my palm.

senses.definition: A smoothing action.
A domestic animal having a smooth coat.
A member of an anti-hippie fashion movement in 1970s Britain.
The analysis obtained through a smoothing procedure.

core.definition: Having an even surface or texture with no lumps, bumps, or roughness.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the long oo sound, and the th is voiced, so it is a soft buzzing th as in 'this'. Keep the final sound clearly voiced.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, since smooth suggests pleasant texture, taste, or ease. It can be negative when describing a person who is too polished or slick, such as a smooth talker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smooth constantly for textures and tastes, such as a smooth peanut butter or a smooth sauce. In food talk, a smooth drink has no lumps and is mild and easy to drink. Calling someone smooth usually means they are charming, though it can suggest they are too slick to trust.

distinctions.note: Silky suggests a fine, soft, luxurious feel, while smooth only means free of roughness or lumps.
Creamy describes richness and fat content, while smooth describes an even texture without lumps.

examples.everyday: This peanut butter is so smooth, not chunky at all.
examples.professional: The new interface gives users a smooth experience when they switch between screens.
examples.analytical: A smooth function has continuous derivatives, so its graph contains no sharp corners or breaks.

nuance.analogy: A smooth surface is like a freshly paved road with no potholes.
nuance.etymology: From Old English smoþ, meaning even or free of roughness.
common_mistakes: Saying 'smooth' for a person's voice meaning 'smoothly' in a sentence, as in 'he talks smooth'; the correct form is 'smoothly' for actions.
Pronouncing the vowel as the short sound in 'book' instead of the long oo in 'food'.

smooth.etymology: From Middle English *smothe*, *smethe*, from Old English *smēþe*, *smōþ*, both from **smanþī*, of unknown origin.

conversation.text: Blend the soup until it's smooth.
I like smooth peanut butter better than crunchy.
This coffee is really smooth, not bitter at all.

senses.definition: Inclined to sniffle.
senses.example: I've been sniffly all weekend; I think I've caught a cold.

senses.definition: Resembling a sniffle.
senses.example: a sniffly sound

core.definition: Having a runny or stuffy nose and sniffing a lot, usually because of a mild cold or allergies.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and it has two syllables, not three. Because the l is followed by a vowel, it is a regular l, so the word is 'SNIF-lee' with no extra vowel between f and l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, and usually used sympathetically about someone who is sick.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sniffly' in casual talk to describe someone with a cold or allergies, often a child. It is most common in the phrase 'feeling sniffly' or in describing a sniffly kid. A natural reply is 'Feel better soon.'

distinctions.note: Stuffy describes a blocked nose; sniffly describes the sniffing and runny nose that often come with it.
Sniffy means snobbish or disdainful, so it is a different word with a very different meaning.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm a little sniffly today, so I'll keep my distance from the coffee machine.
examples.professional: I'm working from home today because I'm sniffly, but I can still review the pull request this afternoon.
examples.analytical: The sniffly quality of his voice in the recording made the testimony sound more sincere to the jury.

nuance.analogy: Being sniffly is like having a faucet that drips steadily until the cold passes.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sniffle with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel between the f and l and saying three syllables; say SNIF-lee.
Confusing 'sniffly' with 'sniffy', which means snobbish.

senses.definition: So named; commonly called.
senses.example: the so-called Ising mode

senses.definition: Commonly called by such a name, but false or unfitting.
senses.example: These so-called "assistants" are making our jobs harder, not easier!

core.definition: Called by that name, often when the name is doubtful, unfair or false.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SOH. The second word is lighter, and the -ed is not a separate syllable, so it sounds like 'kawld'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or skeptical, because it signals doubt about the label; neutral when it simply names a term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'so-called' in news, debates and arguments to signal doubt about a label, as in 'the so-called experts'. It can sound dismissive, so use it carefully, especially in polite conversation. It is hyphenated before a noun, never after it.

distinctions.note: Alleged refers to an unproven accusation or claim; so-called questions the label itself rather than the facts.
Supposed means believed to be true, often without proof; so-called more clearly names a term and doubts it.
Self-styled means someone calls themselves by a title; so-called doubts a label that others give.

examples.everyday: I'm done with his so-called help; he just makes things worse.
examples.professional: We should stop using the so-called quick wins label in status reports, because nothing about those tasks is quick.
examples.analytical: The so-called natural order of the universe, Hume argued, rests on habit rather than demonstrable necessity.

nuance.analogy: 'So-called' is like putting quotation marks around a word in your voice: you repeat the label but signal you do not fully accept it.
nuance.etymology: From so (in this way) plus called, literally named in this way.
common_mistakes: Writing it without the hyphen before a noun, as in 'so called experts'
Using it neutrally when you actually doubt the label, which can sound sarcastic to listeners

senses.definition: Lather, suds, foam produced by soap in water.

core.definition: The foam or bubbles that form when soap mixes with water, especially while washing dishes or hands.

pronunciation.tip: 'Soap' has secondary stress and 'suds' has primary stress. The final s in 'suds' is voiced like a z, so say SUDZ, not 'sudz' with a hard s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday; it is often used in a light, descriptive way.
nuance.usage_note: 'Soap suds' is a very common American phrase for the foam from washing, used in kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry. Americans also use 'suds' alone in casual talk, as in 'I'm up to my elbows in suds.' Avoid calling it 'soap foam' or 'soap bubbles,' which sound unnatural.

distinctions.note: Foam is a general word for bubbles in any liquid, while soap suds specifically refers to foam made by soap.
Lather is the soapy foam itself or the act of covering something with it; suds is more casual and common in everyday speech.

collocations: a sink full of soap suds

examples.everyday: I've got soap suds all over my hands, can you grab me a towel?
examples.professional: The new dish detergent produces fewer soap suds, so the industrial dishwasher rinses cleaner.
examples.analytical: Soap suds are a colloid of gas bubbles stabilized by a film of surfactant molecules at the water surface.

nuance.analogy: Soap suds are like a crowd of tiny balloons, each wall made of soap molecules holding air inside.
nuance.etymology: Soap is from Old English sāpe; the origin of 'suds' is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'soap foams' or 'soap bubbles' for suds; 'soap suds' is the usual American term.
Pronouncing 'suds' with an unvoiced s (SUDS); the final sound is a voiced z.

senses.definition: A ball that is designed for use in the sport of soccer; a football.
senses.example: The kids kicked the soccer ball across the field until the sun went down.

core.definition: A round ball used to play soccer, kicked with the feet; only goalkeepers may use their hands on it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BAWL, the second word. In soccer the first syllable has a weak secondary stress, and the final -er is a light, r-colored vowel, so do not add an extra 'ah' after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and purely descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say soccer ball for the round ball used in the sport, and soccer is the everyday word for the game in the United States. Football here means American football, so saying football ball would confuse people. Outside the US, the same ball is called a football.

distinctions.note: In American usage football means American football; the sport called football in Britain is called soccer here.
A volleyball is hit over a net with the hands and is a different sport, so do not call a volleyball a soccer ball.

examples.everyday: Grab the soccer ball from the trunk, we're heading to the park.
examples.professional: Can you check whether the soccer balls for the company picnic have shipped this week?
examples.analytical: A soccer ball's size, pressure, and panel design shape how the game feels, which is why sports scientists measure them closely.

nuance.analogy: Like a basketball kicked instead of dribbled: the same challenge of control, with the feet doing the work.
nuance.etymology: Soccer was shortened in 19th-century England from association football; ball is an Old English word.
common_mistakes: Saying football ball, which Americans would take to mean an American football; say soccer ball.
Stressing the second syllable of soccer as in 'sah-KER'; the stress belongs on the first syllable of the word.

senses.definition: Of or relating to sodomy.

core.definition: Of or relating to sodomy, a term used mainly in historical, legal or technical discussion of sexual acts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -DAH-, and the first vowel is a reduced schwa. Avoid stressing the first syllable, as in SOD-ik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is a technical or legal term, but it has historically been used to condemn people, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet this adjective in legal histories, academic writing on the history of law, or older court records. Americans rarely use it in everyday speech, and in casual talk they would avoid it. When discussing the topic today, most people use more neutral terms and describe the specific act instead.

examples.professional: The legal brief quoted the nineteenth-century statute, which used the sodomic offense as a catch-all category.
examples.analytical: Early modern courts often applied sodomic laws to a wide range of acts that the statutes never clearly defined.

nuance.analogy: Think of sodomic as a legal label from an old filing cabinet: it names a category, but the label itself tells you little about the actual events inside.
nuance.etymology: Derived from sodomy, from Sodom, the city in Genesis 19, plus the suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (SOD-ik) instead of the second (suh-DAH-mik).
Using it casually as a general insult, which sounds archaic and hostile in American conversation.

senses.definition: To express (a psychological process) through physical symptoms such as pain or anxiety; to have a psychosomatic reaction to (e.g. a situation).

core.definition: To express psychological distress or emotional conflict through physical symptoms such as pain, fatigue or stomach trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH, and reduce the middle syllable to a schwa. The final -ize is pronounced like the word eyes, not like eez.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to clinical. It can sound dismissive if applied to a specific person, so describe patterns rather than judge individuals.
nuance.usage_note: Somatize is used mostly in clinical and academic writing about how people express emotional stress through the body. Americans in everyday talk would say my stress goes into my body or I get physical symptoms when I am anxious. The term is less common in casual conversation and can sound clinical or judgmental if used about a friend.

distinctions.note: Psychosomatic is an adjective describing an illness with mental and physical roots, while somatize is a verb describing the process of expressing distress through the body.
Exaggerate means overstating symptoms on purpose, while somatize describes a real physical experience caused by psychological distress.

examples.everyday: I tend to somatize when I'm worried; my shoulders knot up the night before every big exam.
examples.professional: Some patients somatize their grief, so we ask about emotional history during the physical exam.
examples.analytical: Whether a culture encourages people to somatize distress may shape which symptoms are taken as legitimate medical complaints.

nuance.analogy: Like pressure in a closed pipe finding the weakest joint, distress can leak out through the body when it has no other outlet.
nuance.etymology: From Greek soma, body, plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling somatise; American writing uses -ize.
Stressing the last syllable (soh-muh-TYZE) instead of the first.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or producing soot.
senses.example: The sooty exhaust from the old diesel truck hung over the highway all morning.

senses.definition: Soiled with soot.
Of the color of soot.
To blacken or make dirty with soot.
senses.example: The kerosene lamp kept sootying the glass chimney, so she cleaned it every evening.

core.definition: Covered with soot or stained by it, or having the dark gray or black color of soot.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable has the short oo vowel, as in 'book', and the second syllable is a light ee. Do not stretch the first vowel into a long sound like 'soot' in 'boot'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests dirt, grime or damage from smoke or fire.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sooty for chimneys, fireplaces, engines, faces and hands after work with fire or coal. It is common in both casual speech and reports. Sooty often describes a surface, but in casual talk people might also say dirty or grimy if the stain is not from fire.

distinctions.note: Dirty is a general word for anything unclean, while sooty specifically means covered with soot from burning.
Grimy refers to dirt built up on a surface over time, while sooty specifically refers to black residue from burning.
Smoky means full of smoke or smelling of smoke, while sooty means covered with the black particles that smoke leaves behind.

examples.everyday: After we cleaned out the old fireplace, my hands were so sooty that I had to scrub them twice.
examples.professional: The inspection report noted sooty exhaust stains around the boiler vent, which suggests incomplete combustion.
examples.analytical: The sooty haze over the mill town became a visible symbol of early industrial pollution.

nuance.analogy: A sooty pot is like a campfire kettle that has been used so often that it carries the dark marks of every fire.
nuance.etymology: From soot, with the adjective-forming suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as a long oo, as in 'boot', rather than the short vowel of 'book'.
Using sooty for any dirt, when it specifically refers to soot from burning.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to South Asia.
A native or inhabitant of South Asia.
senses.example: The chef, a South Asian who grew up in New Jersey, taught me to make dal from scratch.

core.definition: Of or relating to South Asia, the region including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and nearby countries.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'Asian', with a weaker stress on 'South'. In American speech, 'Asian' has the 'zh' sound, as in 'measure', in the middle, so avoid making it a hard 'sh' or a 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and respectful; it is the standard term for the region and for people from it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'South Asian' for the region and for people of South Asian heritage, and it is common in census, academic and workplace settings. When you know someone's country, it is more precise to say 'Indian' or 'Pakistani', and you should not assume a person's background from their appearance. Use the term carefully and do not use it to describe people who are not from that region.

distinctions.note: Indian refers specifically to India or its people; South Asian covers several countries, so use Indian when the nationality is known.
Southeast Asia is a different region, including countries such as Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia; do not mix the two up.
Subcontinental is a geographical term for the Indian subcontinent; South Asian is the broader, more common term in American usage.

examples.everyday: We're going to a South Asian restaurant downtown tonight, and I'm hoping they have the lamb curry.
examples.professional: Our South Asian market team needs a localized version of the app, so please include Hindi and Urdu in the next sprint.
examples.analytical: South Asian history cannot be understood apart from the colonial borders drawn in 1947, which still shape its politics.

nuance.analogy: South Asian is like the word European: it names a large region with many languages, cultures and histories, not a single country.
nuance.etymology: Formed from south and Asian, from Asia, the name of the continent.
common_mistakes: Using 'South Asian' as a nationality; Americans use it for a region, and 'Indian' or 'Pakistani' for a specific country.
Confusing it with 'Southeast Asian', which refers to a different region.

senses.definition: Marked with dots or spots, spotted.
senses.example: The bird's eggs were speckled as camouflage.

senses.definition: Sporadically and irregularly marked.
senses.example: The robin's eggs were pale blue and speckled with small brown spots.

core.definition: Covered with small spots or dots of a different color, such as an egg, a bird, or a face with freckles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-led' is usually reduced to a short 'uld' sound with no separate 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It describes a pattern of spots, often in a pleasant or natural way, such as on eggs, fabric, or animals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use speckled for natural or decorative spots: speckled eggs, a speckled trout, or a speckled granite countertop. It is common in everyday speech and in shopping or cooking contexts. For people with freckles, Americans usually say 'freckled' instead.

distinctions.note: Spotted is more general and can describe large, clear spots, while speckled suggests many tiny dots scattered across a surface.
Freckled is used specifically for small brown spots on human skin, while speckled is used for objects, animals, and surfaces.

examples.everyday: Those eggs from the farm stand are speckled brown, so they look great in the basket.
examples.professional: The client wants a speckled finish on the countertop, so we should confirm the granite sample before ordering.
examples.analytical: The painting's speckled surface suggests a deliberate attempt to imitate the texture of weathered stone.

nuance.analogy: A speckled surface is like a night sky full of tiny stars scattered across dark cloth.
nuance.etymology: From speck, a small spot, with the adjective suffix -led; speck comes from Old English specca.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'speckled' with an extra syllable, as 'speck-uh-led'.
Confusing speckled with specked, which is an uncommon spelling variant; speckled is the standard American spelling.

senses.definition: A person who acts as the voice of another person or a group of people.

core.definition: A person chosen to speak publicly on behalf of an organization, company, government agency or group.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, spokes. The middle syllable is rhotic, so say the r clearly, and the ending is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes an official role and suggests trust and responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use spokesperson as a gender-neutral term for someone who speaks officially for a company, police department or government. You might hear 'The company spokesperson said the recall was voluntary' on the news. Spokesman and spokeswoman are also used, but spokesperson is preferred in most workplaces.

distinctions.note: A representative acts for someone in negotiations or business, while a spokesperson speaks to the public or the press.
Spokeswoman refers specifically to a woman, while spokesperson can refer to anyone.

examples.everyday: My sister works as the spokesperson for the local hospital, so she is always on TV.
examples.professional: Please send all press questions to the company spokesperson so we can give one consistent answer.
examples.analytical: The theologian was not an official spokesperson for the church, yet his letters were read as representing its views.

nuance.analogy: Like a microphone for a group, the spokesperson carries the message without creating it.
nuance.etymology: Compound of spokes, from spoke in the sense of one who speaks, and person, modeled on spokesman.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in spokes-PER-son.
Using spokesperson for a private representative in a negotiation.

senses.definition: (historical) The fancied production of live organisms without previously existing parents from inorganic matter, or from decomposing organic matter, a notion which at one time had many supporters.
senses.example: Pasteur's experiments finally discredited the old theory of spontaneous generation.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: (historical) The discredited idea that living organisms could arise from nonliving matter without parents, as maggots from meat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TAY in 'spontaneous' and RAY in 'generation'. The 'g' in 'generation' is a 'j' sound, and the 'ti' is pronounced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical. In modern science it is considered false, so it can sound outdated or wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in biology courses, history of science and philosophy. Pasteur's experiments in the 1860s disproved it. Modern scientists use abiogenesis for the study of how life first arose from chemistry, which is a different idea. You will rarely hear the phrase in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Abiogenesis is the modern scientific theory that life arose from chemical reactions over long periods; spontaneous generation was the older claim that living things appear quickly and routinely from decay.
Biogenesis is the principle that life comes only from existing life; it is the view that replaced spontaneous generation.

examples.professional: Pasteur's experiments are the reason biology textbooks no longer accept spontaneous generation.
examples.analytical: Medieval naturalists accepted spontaneous generation because their observations seemed to confirm it.

nuance.analogy: Spontaneous generation is like believing a cake could bake itself out of flour on a shelf with no oven: the idea seems to work until someone controls the conditions.
nuance.etymology: Spontaneous from Latin spontaneus, of one's own accord; generation from Latin generatio, from generare, to beget.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase to describe modern science of life's origin; that is abiogenesis.
Pronouncing 'generation' with a schwa-r ending instead of 'jen-uh-RAY-shun'.

senses.definition: A person who observes something.
A member of a sniper team who in addition to this function is responsible for providing additional information about targets from a different point of view.
senses.example: The spotter scanned the ridge through binoculars and radioed the shooter about the target's new position.

senses.definition: One who supervises a person performing an activity, in order to help them should they be unable to complete it.
senses.example: The gym spotter stood behind him, ready to catch the barbell if his arms gave out.

senses.definition: A person who gives directions for a crane or vehicle (that is challenging to navigate) from a different point of view to the moved load.
senses.example: The crane spotter waved his orange flags so the operator could place the steel beam safely.

senses.definition: Dolphins of the genus Stenella, and specifically Stenella attenuata distinguished from the streaker (Stenella coeruleoalba) and the spinner (Stenella longirostris).
senses.example: Marine biologists recorded a pod of spotter dolphins riding the bow waves off Hawaii.

senses.definition: A team member responsible for communication with the driver to keep them up-to-date about on-track events, such as other nearby cars.
senses.example: During the final lap, the spotter warned the driver that a slower car was approaching on the inside.

senses.definition: A person employed to assist a sports presenter by identifying the players or events during a game.
senses.example: The broadcast crew added a spotter who named each player and penalty flag during the game.

core.definition: A person who watches for, notices, or looks out for something, or who stands by to help during an activity such as lifting weights.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and in fast speech the t between vowels flaps, so it sounds almost like 'SPAH-der'. The final -er is a rhotic, unstressed 'ur' sound, and it is only one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a helpful role, though in a sniper or military context it has a technical meaning.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, spotter is most often used in the gym, where a person stands by a lifter to help if the weight becomes too heavy. It is also used for bird watchers, aircraft spotters, and people who look for specific things in a crowd. In military writing it refers to a member of a sniper team, which is more technical.

distinctions.note: A lookout watches for danger or specific movement. A spotter may watch for a specific target or stand by to help someone.
Observer is a general word for someone who watches or studies. Spotter suggests a more active, specific role, often in sports or outdoor activities.

examples.everyday: Can you be my spotter? I'm going to try a heavy bench press today.
examples.professional: We need a spotter on the warehouse floor to catch mislabeled pallets before they leave the dock.
examples.analytical: The analyst served as a spotter, flagging anomalies in the data before the automated model detected them.

nuance.analogy: A spotter is like a lifeguard at a pool: they watch closely so they can help the moment something goes wrong.
nuance.etymology: From spot (verb) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using spotter for a general observer in formal writing, where observer is often more precise.
Confusing spotter with spotlight or with spotty, which have different meanings.

senses.definition: A short, high-pitched sound, as of two objects rubbing together, or the sounds made by mice and other small animals.
A card game similar to group solitaire.
senses.example: After dinner, the family sat down to play squeak, their favorite card game.

senses.definition: A narrow squeak.
senses.example: We escaped the collision with a squeak, missing the truck by inches.

senses.definition: To emit a short, high-pitched sound.
senses.example: The old porch door squeaked every time someone walked across the threshold.

senses.definition: To inform, to squeal.
senses.example: Someone in the crew squeaked to the police about the warehouse thefts.

senses.definition: To speak or sound in a high-pitched manner.
senses.example: Our tiny neighbor squeaked with delight when she saw the puppies.

senses.definition: To empty the pile of 13 cards a player deals to oneself in the card game of the same name.
senses.example: She finally squeaked after moving the last card from her thirteen-card pile.

senses.definition: To win or progress by a narrow margin.
senses.example: Our team squeaked into the playoffs with a one-point win in the final game.

core.definition: A short, high-pitched sound, like a door hinge, a shoe or a small animal.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a long EE sound. End with a hard k, and don't turn the word into 'skwick' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for objects and animals; it can sound childish or nervous when describing a person's voice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use squeak for thin, sharp sounds from hinges, toys, shoes or mice. The phrases 'squeak by' and 'a narrow squeak' mean barely succeeding or narrowly avoiding trouble, and they are common in casual talk about exams or money. Used for a person's voice, it sounds high and small.

distinctions.note: A squeal is louder and more piercing, often from pain, fear or excitement; a squeak is smaller and softer.
A creak is a low, drawn-out sound from an old door or floor; a squeak is higher and sharper.

examples.everyday: The old screen door gives a squeak every time someone opens it.
examples.professional: The report passed review, but only by a squeak after the late revisions.
examples.analytical: A squeak of dissent ran through the committee, though no one spoke openly against the proposal.

nuance.analogy: A squeak is like a tiny, sharp hinge sound that catches your attention.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a thin, high sound; from Middle English squeken.
common_mistakes: Using squeak for a loud scream, where squeal fits better
Dropping the final k or pronouncing it as a t

senses.definition: A single step in a staircase.
senses.example: She missed the bottom stair and nearly twisted her ankle on the hardwood floor.

senses.definition: A series of steps; a staircase.
senses.example: The narrow stair led up to the attic where the old trunks were kept.

core.definition: One of the steps in a set that you climb to go up or down between floors.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds like stare or stair in American English, with the r clearly pronounced. Do not add an extra vowel after the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stair for a single step, and staircase for the whole structure. In everyday talk people often say the stairs, the stairway, or the steps. Use one stair only when you mean an individual step.

distinctions.note: Step is more general and can mean a single movement or a stage; stair is specifically one tread in a staircase.
Staircase is the whole structure with its steps and railings; stair is one step.

examples.everyday: Be careful, the bottom stair is loose, so hold the railing.
examples.professional: The building code requires a handrail on every stair with more than four risers.
examples.analytical: Each stair in the old chapel marks a step toward the altar, turning the climb into a small pilgrimage.

nuance.analogy: Like one rung on a ladder: a single step that, combined with others, takes you somewhere new.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stæger, stair, related to stige, to climb.
common_mistakes: Saying one stair when you mean the whole staircase.
Using stairs and stair interchangeably in precise contexts.

stair.etymology: From Middle English *steire*, *staire*, *stayre*, *stayer*, *steir*, *steyre*, *steyer*, from Old English *stǣġer* (“stair, staircase”), from **staigri*, from Proto-Germanic **staigriz* (“stairs, scaffolding”), from Proto-Indo-European **steygʰ-* (“to…

senses.definition: A flight of stairs; a stairway.
A connected set of flights of stairs; a stairwell.
A set of locks (enclosed sections of waterway) mounted one above the next.
senses.example: The canal's staircase of locks lifts barges nearly sixty feet up the hillside.

senses.definition: To modify (a signal, a graph, etc.) to reduce a smooth curve to a series of discrete steps.
senses.example: The plotting script staircases the smooth curve into eight discrete steps for the report.

senses.definition: To increase one's share in a co-ownership.
senses.example: Over the years, she staircased her stake in the apartment building until she held a majority.

core.definition: A set of stairs, with its railings and supports, that connects the floors of a building.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on case. Pronounce the r clearly and do not say stay-case; it is one word, not stair case.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; sometimes positive when describing a grand or handsome feature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say staircase or stairs for indoor steps in a house or building. Staircase is slightly more formal and often refers to the whole structure, including railings, as in 'a curved staircase.' Stairway is more common for outdoor or open steps, and stairwell refers to the enclosed shaft.

distinctions.note: Stairs is the everyday word for the steps; staircase often includes the structure and railing.
Stairway usually means a route of steps, often outdoors; staircase suggests a built architectural feature.
Stairwell is the enclosed vertical space around the steps, important for fire safety; staircase is the steps themselves.

examples.everyday: Watch your step on the staircase, the carpet is loose near the bottom.
examples.professional: The renovation moves the staircase to the center of the lobby to improve foot traffic.
examples.analytical: In Gothic architecture the staircase often became a symbol of ascent from ordinary life toward a higher order.

nuance.analogy: A staircase is like a ladder built for comfort, with a steady rhythm that lets your legs do the work.
nuance.etymology: From stair (Old English stæger, step) plus case (enclosure or frame).
common_mistakes: Writing stair case as two words in formal writing; it is one word.
Putting the main stress on the second syllable; say STAIR-kays.

senses.definition: A person who takes part in stamp collecting.
An officer who collects stamp duties.

core.definition: A person who collects postage stamps as a hobby, usually arranging them in albums by country, year or design.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEK in collector, while stamp has a lighter secondary stress. Say the mp cleanly, and keep the final er light rather than a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a friendly, traditional hobby.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say stamp collector or stamp collecting for this hobby in everyday talk. Philatelist is the formal term used by experts and clubs. The second dictionary sense, an official who collects stamp duties, is historical and rarely heard today.

distinctions.note: Philatelist is the formal or expert term for a stamp collector; in everyday conversation Americans say stamp collector.
A numismatist collects coins and paper money rather than stamps.

examples.everyday: My grandpa was a stamp collector, and he spent every Sunday sorting his albums.
examples.professional: Our client is a serious stamp collector who wants the appraisal to meet auction house standards.
examples.analytical: A stamp collector's album can serve as an archive of national history, since each issue reflects the politics and art of its era.

nuance.analogy: A stamp collector is like a librarian of tiny paper histories, sorting each issue by country, year and design.
nuance.etymology: Stamp from Middle English stampe; collector from Latin collector, one who gathers.
common_mistakes: Using the plural stamps collector; the usual compound is stamp collector.
Using philatelist in casual talk, where it sounds formal or like a technical label.

senses.definition: A measure of how likely a mean of means is to be wrong. It is the standard deviation of the sample sizes in each to the sample means.
senses.example: The standard error of our survey mean was small, so we trusted the estimate.

core.definition: The standard deviation of a sample statistic, such as the mean, across repeated samples; it estimates how much that statistic would vary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'error', so it sounds like 'AIR-er'. The r in 'error' is pronounced clearly in American speech, and 'standard' is reduced to 'stan-derd'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise statistical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in research papers, data science reports and polls, often as 'SE' or with a confidence interval. Be careful: it does not mean an error in the everyday sense of a mistake. Professionals say 'the standard error of the mean' when precision is the topic.

distinctions.note: Standard deviation measures spread of individual data points, while standard error measures spread of a sample statistic across samples.
Margin of error is usually about 1.96 times the standard error for a 95 percent confidence interval, so it is a related but different quantity.

examples.everyday: The poll says 52 percent, but the standard error is about 2 points, so it could be closer to a tie.
examples.professional: Our churn estimate looks precise, but the standard error is wide because the sample only covers one region.
examples.analytical: A small standard error does not guarantee an unbiased estimate; it only reflects sampling variability under the assumed model.

nuance.analogy: Like asking many different groups of people for their average height: the standard error tells you how much those averages would jump around.
nuance.etymology: 'Standard' from Old French estandart; 'error' from Latin errare, 'to wander'. The term is from twentieth-century statistics.
common_mistakes: Treating standard error as a measure of a single mistake or bias.
Confusing it with standard deviation, which describes the data rather than the estimate.

senses.definition: Begin a meal with something: "We'll start off with the calamari."

core.definition: To begin a meal or activity with a particular item or step.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OFF, not on start. The word with usually reduces to a weak 'with,' and the words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It sounds natural in restaurants and social settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression when ordering or planning a meal, as in 'We'll start off with the calamari.' At a restaurant, a server might ask 'Would you like to start off with something?' A natural reply is 'Sure, we'll start with the appetizers.' It can also refer to any activity, such as a meeting agenda.

distinctions.note: Start with is simpler and more general, while start off with is more conversational and often used for the first course or item.

examples.everyday: Can we start off with a couple of appetizers while we look at the menu?
examples.professional: Let's start off with a quick round of updates before we get into the roadmap.
examples.analytical: Plato's dialogues often start off with a simple question that gradually exposes deeper confusion.

nuance.analogy: Starting off with an appetizer is like opening a door before walking into the main room.
nuance.etymology: Start comes from Old English styrtan, meaning to leap or jump.
common_mistakes: Saying 'start off' without with when a specific item follows, as in 'start off the calamari.'
Stressing start instead of off.

conversation.text: Let's start off with some appetizers.
I'll start off with the soup, please.
We started off with drinks at the bar.

senses.definition: A system to decrease turnaround time at terminal stations where a second driver enters the rear cab of an arriving train and departs driving the train from that end while the first driver is walking the length of the platform ready to take over the subsequent departure.
senses.example: The rail operator adopted stepping back at the terminal to cut turnaround time for trains.

core.definition: The act of moving backward a step, or of withdrawing from a role or involvement to gain perspective.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on BACK, and the -ing is a reduced syllable with a short ih sound. Keep the t in step unreleased and make the final k clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means reflection or stepping away to rest; negative when it means withdrawing from a responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'taking a step back' rather than 'stepping back' as a noun. In railroads, stepping back is a technical term for a quick crew change at a terminal. In everyday talk, the gerund form appears in phrases like 'stepping back from management,' meaning to give up a role.

distinctions.note: Retreating suggests a withdrawal under pressure, often military or defeat; stepping back is usually calmer and chosen.
Stepping away usually means leaving a task or place for a while; stepping back also includes a shift in perspective.

examples.everyday: Stepping back from the argument helped me see that we both wanted the same thing for the kids.
examples.professional: Stepping back from direct management let our lead engineer own the roadmap, and the team moved faster.
examples.analytical: Stepping back from the text to consider its historical setting clarifies what the author was actually trying to say.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker pausing on the trail to look at the whole valley instead of the next rock.
nuance.etymology: The gerund of step back, from step (Old English stæppan) and back (Old English bæc).
common_mistakes: Using stepping back as a verb of motion in place of the phrase is stepping back; learners often drop the auxiliary.
Confusing the everyday sense with the railroad term; in most conversations it means pausing or withdrawing.

senses.definition: One who stinks.
senses.example: Skunks are the worst stinkers in the animal kingdom.

senses.definition: A contemptible person or thing.
Something difficult (e.g. a given puzzle) or unpleasant (e.g. negative review, nasty letter).
senses.example: Today's crossword is a stinker.

senses.definition: Any of several species of large Antarctic petrels which feed on blubber and carrion and have an offensive odor, such as the giant fulmar.
A chemist.
A western gray kangaroo.
A giant petrel.
An eastern long-necked turtle (which emits a foul-smelling musk when threatened).

core.definition: An informal term for a very unpleasant, mean, or difficult person, thing, or problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ng' before 'k' is one nasal sound, so do not add a separate 'g' or 'n'; end with a clear American 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Negative but often playful. Calling a child a 'little stinker' is affectionate, while calling a test or review a 'stinker' is simply complaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'you little stinker' playfully to a child who is naughty, and 'that test was a stinker' to mean it was very hard. It is informal, so avoid it in professional writing or with people you want to impress. A natural reply to 'That was a stinker' is 'Tell me about it' or 'Yeah, it was rough'.

distinctions.note: 'Jerk' is more offensive and directly insulting; 'stinker' is milder and often playful.
'Rat' means someone who betrays others; 'stinker' is a general word for an unpleasant person or thing.
A 'troublemaker' causes conflict; a 'stinker' can be a hard test, a bad review, or a playful naughty child.

examples.everyday: You little stinker, you ate the last cookie and then said it wasn't you!
examples.professional: The Q3 forecast is a stinker, so we need to reset expectations with leadership before the meeting.
examples.analytical: Some arguments in philosophy are stinkers: they look elegant until you press on one premise.

nuance.analogy: Like a stinky sock in a clean wash, a stinker spoils the mood for everything around it.
nuance.etymology: From stink plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'stinker' only for a bad smell; in everyday American English it usually means an unpleasant or difficult person or thing.
Pronouncing it 'STIN-ker' and dropping the 'ng' sound, or adding an extra 'g' ('STING-gah').

senses.definition: A store or supply.
senses.example: We have a stock of televisions on hand.

senses.definition: A store of goods ready for sale; inventory.
senses.example: We have a stock of televisions on hand.

senses.definition: A supply of anything, stored until used; especially, such a supply that is ready for use.
senses.example: Lay in a stock of wood for the winter season.

senses.definition: A stack of undealt cards made available to the players.
The population of a given type of animal (especially fish) available to be captured from the wild for economic use.
senses.example: The stocks of this fishery are recovering from overfishing, but the gains can easily reverse if our husbandry efforts lapse.

senses.definition: The capital raised by a company through the issue of shares; the total of shares held by an individual shareholder.
senses.example: His grandpa had bought some stock in General Electric in 1905, and he refused to sell it ever after.

senses.definition: A share in a company.
The price or value of the stock of a company on the stock market.
senses.example: When the bad news came out, the company's stock dropped precipitously.

senses.definition: Railroad rolling stock.
senses.example: The Grand Trunk Railway had just purchased a large order of stock from the American Car and Foundry Company.

senses.definition: Farm or ranch animals; livestock.
senses.example: Good ranchers must continually keep watch over the health of their stock.

senses.definition: The measure of how highly a person or institution is valued.
senses.example: After that last screw-up of mine, my stock is pretty low around here.

senses.definition: Any of several types of security that are similar to a stock, or marketed like one.
The raw material from which things are made, such as feedstock.
senses.example: They make beef stock from the butchery scraps that they otherwise might not have used.

senses.definition: Broth made from meat (originally bones) or vegetables, used as a basis for stew or soup.
senses.example: They make beef stock from the butchery scraps that they otherwise might not have used.

senses.definition: The type of paper used in printing.
senses.example: The books were printed on a heavier stock this year.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of film stock.
Plain soap before it is colored and perfumed.
Stock theater, summer stock theater.
The trunk and woody main stems or limbs of a tree; the base from which something grows or branches.
The plant upon which the scion is grafted.
Lineage; family; ancestry.
A larger grouping of language families: a superfamily or macrofamily.
Any of the several species of cruciferous flowers in the genus Matthiola.
A handle or stem to which the working part of an implement or weapon is attached.
The part of a rifle or shotgun that rests against the shooter's shoulder.
The handle of a whip, fishing rod, etc.
Part of a machine that supports items or holds them in place.
The headstock of a lathe, drill, etc.
The tailstock of a lathe.
A bar, stick, or rod. A ski pole.
A ski pole.
A type of (now formal or official) neckwear.
A necktie or cravat, particularly a wide necktie popular in the eighteenth century, often seen today as a part of formal wear for horse riding competitions.
A piece of black cloth worn under a clerical collar.
A bed for infants; a crib, cot, or cradle.
A piece of wood magically made to be just like a real baby and substituted for it by magical beings.
A block of wood; something fixed and solid; a pillar; a firm support; a post.
The frame or timbers on which a ship rests during construction.
Red and gray bricks, used for the exterior of walls and the front of buildings.
The beater of a fulling mill.
A thrust with a rapier; a stoccado.
A bar going through an anchor, perpendicular to the flukes.
The axle attached to the rudder, which transfers the movement of the helm to the rudder.
A pipe (vertical cylinder of ore)
In tectology, an aggregate or colony of individuals, such as trees, chains of salpae, etc.
To provide with material requisites; to store; to fill; to supply.
senses.example: to stock a warehouse with goods

senses.definition: To have on hand for sale.
senses.example: The store stocks all kinds of dried vegetables.

senses.definition: To allow (cows) to retain milk for twenty-four hours or more prior to sale.
To put in the stocks as punishment.
To fit (an anchor) with a stock, or to fasten the stock firmly in place.
(dated) To arrange cards in a certain manner for cheating purposes; to stack the deck.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Of a type normally available for purchase/in stock.
senses.example: stock items

senses.definition: Having the same configuration as cars sold to the non-racing public, or having been modified from such a car.
Straightforward, ordinary, just another, very basic.
senses.example: He gave me a stock answer.

core.definition: A flavorful liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables, used as a base for soups, sauces and gravies.

pronunciation.tip: Americans pronounce the vowel as a short open ah, with no glide, and the final k is crisp and unaspirated. Most American speakers do not distinguish it from stalk in everyday speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday. It is a positive word in cooking, suggesting homemade quality.
nuance.usage_note: In American cooking, stock usually means a liquid made from bones or vegetables, while broth is often a lighter, seasoned liquid meant to be sipped or used as is. Recipes call for chicken stock or vegetable stock, and cooks often make it at home. A natural conversation about soup is Did you use homemade stock or store-bought?

distinctions.note: Broth is usually a thinner, seasoned liquid that can be eaten on its own, while stock is a base ingredient that is rarely served plain.
Bouillon is often a clear, seasoned broth, and in American stores it usually means concentrated cubes or powders.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a carton of chicken stock on your way home? I want to make soup tonight.
examples.professional: For the catering order, we'll use a veal stock base so the sauces stay consistent across locations.
examples.analytical: The stock reduces during simmering, concentrating its flavor the way long reflection concentrates a thought.

nuance.analogy: Like the foundation of a house: you never serve it alone, but everything rests on it.
nuance.etymology: Old English stocc, a tree trunk or stump.
common_mistakes: Confusing stock with broth when ordering in a restaurant.
Saying stocks when you mean one carton of stock, since stocks usually means shares or investments.

stock.etymology: From Middle English *stok*, from Old English *stocc*, from **stokk*, from Proto-Germanic **stukkaz* (“tree-trunk”).

conversation.text: Use chicken stock instead of water for the rice.
Homemade stock is better than canned.
Sorry, that item is out of stock right now.
My dad has been buying tech stocks for years.

senses.definition: Something spoken to fill up an uncomfortable pause in speech; a filled pause or filler.
senses.example: Her constant um and you know were a stopgap while she searched for the next word.

senses.definition: A short-term fix or temporary measure used until something better can be obtained; that which serves as an expedient in an emergency; a band-aid solution.
senses.example: The small company used their old product with a few kludged enhancements as a stopgap until they could develop a new product.

senses.definition: A person appointed or hired to fill a position temporarily until a permanent appointment or hire can be made; a temp.
senses.example: The agency sent a stopgap to cover the receptionist during her maternity leave.

senses.definition: (rare) That which stops up or fills a gap or hole.
senses.example: A folded cardboard sheet was a stopgap in the broken window until the glass arrived.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Short-term; temporary.
senses.example: They put a stopgap solution in place, but need something more permanent.

senses.definition: Filling a gap or pause. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The stopgap measures kept the clinic open until new funding arrived.

senses.definition: To stop up or fill (a physical gap or hole, or a hiatus).
senses.example: We stopgapped the leaking pipe with epoxy until the plumber could replace it.

senses.definition: To use something as a short-term fix or temporary measure until a better alternative can be obtained.
senses.example: The city stopgapped its budget shortfall with one-time transfers from reserve funds.

senses.definition: To work at a position temporarily until a permanent appointment or hire is made.
senses.example: She stopgapped as office manager for three months until the board hired someone permanent.

core.definition: A temporary fix or substitute used until a better solution becomes available.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on the second. The vowel in 'stop' is an open 'ah', not 'aw', and the final p should be crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It signals that something is temporary and not ideal, though acceptable for now.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stopgap constantly at work and at home, for things like a temporary repair, a short-term staffing fix, or a cheap solution before a real purchase. It is informal enough for meetings but not stiff. A natural reply is 'Sure, let's use that as a stopgap for now.'

distinctions.note: Makeshift describes something improvised from whatever is at hand; stopgap emphasizes that it is temporary and will be replaced.
A band-aid solution is more critical, implying it treats symptoms without fixing the underlying problem; a stopgap may be a reasonable short-term choice.

examples.everyday: Our old printer died, so we're using the library's for now as a stopgap.
examples.professional: The team added a manual check as a stopgap while engineers rebuild the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Such policies function as stopgaps, addressing immediate pressures while deferring structural reform.

nuance.analogy: A stopgap is like a piece of tape on a leaking pipe: it holds until the plumber comes.
nuance.etymology: From stop plus gap, literally something that stops up a gap.
common_mistakes: Writing 'stop gap' as two words; the standard form is one word, 'stopgap'.
Using stopgap for a permanent solution; by definition it is temporary.

stopgap.etymology: The noun is derived from *stop* + *gap*, from the phrase to stop a gap.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being submissive.
senses.example: Her quiet submissiveness during the negotiation surprised everyone who knew how firmly she usually argued.

core.definition: The quality of readily yielding to others' authority or wishes, often without resistance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIS, the second syllable. The final -ness is a weak nus sound, and the middle syllable -siv is quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, implying a lack of confidence or independence. It can be positive in religious or respectful contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use submissiveness in psychology, sociology, relationship advice and sometimes education, to describe a personality trait or pattern of behavior. Calling a person submissiveness directly is blunt and can sound insulting. Saying 'she tends to be very accommodating' is often a gentler choice in conversation.

distinctions.note: Obedience means following rules or commands, while submissiveness is a broader attitude or temperament of yielding.
Meekness describes gentle strength under control and can be positive, while submissiveness more often implies weakness or passivity.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog shows so much submissiveness around the big cat that it always backs away.
examples.professional: The review noted a pattern of submissiveness in negotiations, so we coached her to speak up earlier.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the submissiveness of the colonized reflected genuine consent or a strategy of survival.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant that bends in the wind; it survives the storm, but it does not stand its ground.
nuance.etymology: From submissive, from Latin submittere (to lower or put under), plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing submissiveness, a personal trait, with submission, which is the act of yielding.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second, or pronouncing -ness with a full vowel.

senses.definition: The party on whose behalf another party (the subrogee) acts in a subrogation.

core.definition: The party whose rights are passed on to another party, usually the insured person, who has been paid by an insurer for a loss.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GOR, the final syllable, and the -or ending is a clear American r-colored vowel. Do not say it as 'GOOR.' Keep the middle 'ruh' weak and short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in legal and insurance settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subrogor in insurance and legal writing, usually in a formal document, a settlement letter, or a court filing. People in everyday life rarely use it; they refer to the insured person or 'the policyholder.' When the term appears, it is usually paired with subrogee.

distinctions.note: The subrogor is the party whose rights are transferred; the subrogee is the party who acts on those rights.
The insured is the policyholder in general; the subrogor is the insured in the specific setting where rights are transferred after payment.

examples.everyday: The claims representative explained that I am the subrogor here, so the insurer will handle recovery from the other driver.
examples.professional: Before we settle, confirm that the subrogor has not signed a release, since any settlement it makes can impair our recovery.
examples.analytical: In subrogation, the subrogor's rights pass to the subrogee, so the subrogor may not compromise the claim in a way that prejudices the insurer.

nuance.analogy: The subrogor is like a person who hands over a claim ticket to a friend who pays for the repair and then collects the refund.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subrogare, 'to choose as a substitute,' with the -or ending for the party whose rights are transferred.
common_mistakes: Mixing up subrogor and subrogee, which play opposite roles in the transfer.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'GOO' instead of the American r-colored 'GOR.'

senses.definition: A subset of a space which is a space in its own right.
Any (often unspecified) method of communicating or traveling faster than light speed.
senses.example: The novel's starships rely on subspace radio to talk with distant colonies instantly.

senses.definition: An alternative dimension or universe, access to or use of which permits faster-than-light travel or communications; hyperspace.
senses.example: In the old science fiction series, starships vanished into subspace to escape pursuing enemy fleets.

senses.definition: The psychological state of the submissive or bottom during sadomasochistic activity.
senses.example: After the scene, she described drifting into subspace as calming and surprisingly peaceful.

core.definition: In mathematics, a subset of a larger space that itself satisfies the rules of a space, such as a line inside a plane.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SUB. Keep the word as one smooth unit with no pause between sub and space, and make the final s clearly voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical term with no emotional charge in mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: In American mathematics courses and research, subspace is standard for a subset that is closed under the space's operations, especially in linear algebra and topology. Outside technical work, the word is rare, and in science fiction it sometimes refers to hyperspace. When talking with colleagues, specify which kind of subspace you mean, such as a linear subspace or a topological subspace.

distinctions.note: Every subspace is a subset, but a subset need not satisfy the structural rules of the larger space, so subspace is the stronger term.
In mathematics, subspace is a precise term for part of a space, while hyperspace in science fiction is an imagined dimension for faster-than-light travel.

examples.everyday: My kid asked what a subspace was, so I told her it's like a flat sheet inside a bigger room.
examples.professional: Before we apply the regression, we need to confirm that the feature vectors lie in a subspace of lower dimension.
examples.analytical: A subspace is defined by closure under addition and scalar multiplication, and this definition is what makes it inherit the structure of the ambient space.

nuance.analogy: A subspace is like a flat sheet of paper placed inside a room: it is smaller, but it has its own geometry.
nuance.etymology: From sub- (under, within) and space, a term used in mathematics from the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using subspace to mean any smaller set, without requiring that it keep the structure of the larger space.
Confusing the word with hyperspace in science fiction when speaking about mathematics.

senses.definition: The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.
senses.example: In this football tournament, three substitutions can be made during the match.

senses.definition: A substitute or replacement.
senses.example: Gary is off this weekend, so Jeff will be his substitution.

senses.definition: The expansion of the lexicon of a language by native means in correspondence to a foreign term.
senses.example: Old English created 'godspell' as a substitution for the Latin evangelium.

senses.definition: The replacement of an atom, or group of atoms, in a compound, with another.
senses.example: The chemist achieved the substitution of a chlorine atom with a methyl group in the molecule.

core.definition: The act of replacing one thing, person, or item with another, often to fill a gap or achieve the same result.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, TOO. The sh in -tion is pronounced like 'sh' in shoe, and the -tion ending is one syllable 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a replacement without judgment, though context can make it positive or negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use substitution in sports, cooking, math, and formal writing, for example making a substitution in a game or a substitution in a recipe. In everyday talk, people often say swap, replacement, or sub. Substitution is slightly formal, so it fits announcements, instructions, and reports better than casual chats.

distinctions.note: Replacement is usually the thing that takes the place of something broken or missing, while substitution emphasizes the act of swapping one thing for another.
An alternative is one option among several choices, while a substitution means one thing has replaced another that was intended to be used.

examples.everyday: The restaurant made a substitution and gave me sweet potato fries instead of regular fries because they ran out.
examples.professional: The vendor proposed a substitution of one component, so we need to check that it meets the same specification before approval.
examples.analytical: A substitution in an argument is valid only if the replacement term preserves the truth of the premises.

nuance.analogy: A substitution is like swapping a stand-in actor into a role: the part still needs to be filled, but the performer is different.
nuance.etymology: From Latin substitutio, from substituere (to put in place of), from sub- (under) and statuere (to set up).
common_mistakes: Using substitution as a verb; the verb is substitute.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a long vowel, so the word sounds like 'sub-stih-TYOO-shun'.
patterns: [C, U] substitution of X for Y

substitution.etymology: From Middle French *substitution*, from Late Latin *substitutio*.

senses.definition: A movie about superheroes.

core.definition: A movie whose main characters are superheroes with extraordinary powers, often based on comic book stories.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEER in superhero and on MOO in movie, so say soo-per-HEER-oh MOO-vee. The -er and -o syllables are quick and reduced, and the rhotic r stays clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lighthearted; it can be praised or mocked depending on the speaker's taste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superhero movie constantly in everyday conversation and entertainment news, usually when discussing films from Marvel or DC. People often say "superhero film" in writing, but movie is more natural in speech. A typical reply is to name a favorite or ask whether someone has seen the latest one.

distinctions.note: An action movie emphasizes fights and stunts in realistic settings, while a superhero movie centers on characters with extraordinary powers.
Comic book movie is a broader category that includes non-superhero stories, while superhero movie refers specifically to films about superheroes.

examples.everyday: Do you want to watch a superhero movie tonight, or something more relaxing?
examples.professional: The studio wants the next superhero movie to open before the summer schedule fills up, so we need the rough cut by Friday.
examples.analytical: The rise of the superhero movie reflects anxieties about institutional power that are expressed through fantasy spectacle.

nuance.analogy: A superhero movie is like a big family cookout: everyone brings a favorite dish, and the flavor comes from the shared spectacle.
nuance.etymology: Superhero comes from super (beyond) plus hero, first used in the 1910s for characters with extraordinary abilities.
common_mistakes: Saying super-hero movie with the wrong stress, putting equal weight on every word.
Dropping the r in hero, as in soo-per-HEE-oh.

conversation.text: Another superhero movie? There's a new one every month.
The kids want to see the new superhero movie.
I'm kind of tired of superhero movies.

senses.definition: An irrational number, especially one expressed using the √ symbol.
A voiceless consonant.
senses.example: Linguistics students learned that the surd consonants p, t, and k involve no vocal cord vibration.

senses.definition: Involving surds, or irrational numbers; not capable of being expressed in rational numbers.
senses.example: a surd expression or quantity; a surd number

senses.definition: Unvoiced; voiceless.
senses.example: Her speech therapist said the final sound in 'cat' should be surd, with no vocal buzz.

core.definition: An irrational number that cannot be written as a simple fraction, especially a root such as the square root of 2, usually shown with a radical sign.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with the r-colored vowel of 'word' and 'heard', so do not add an extra vowel before the r. Do not confuse it with 'sword' (SORD) or 'absurd' (ab-SURD) when speaking.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use surd in algebra and mathematics courses, often in phrases like 'simplify the surd'. In many US classrooms students more often hear 'irrational number' or 'radical', so surd may sound specialized outside algebra. Teachers use it mainly with radical expressions like √2 or √3.

distinctions.note: Irrational number is the general term for any real number that cannot be a ratio of integers, while surd is used mainly for irrational roots and radical expressions.
A radical is the √ symbol or a root expression, while a surd is the irrational value that the radical expresses.
In phonetics, surd is a separate sense meaning a voiceless consonant, which is the same word with a different meaning.

examples.everyday: My kid's homework has surds in it, and honestly I've forgotten what those are.
examples.professional: In the numerical solver we flag any surd result and round it before storing it as a float.
examples.analytical: The Greek discovery that the diagonal of a unit square is incommensurable with its side amounts to recognizing a surd, which shook their assumption that all magnitudes are ratios.

nuance.analogy: Like a decimal that never ends and never repeats, a surd keeps going without settling into a pattern.
nuance.etymology: From Latin surdus, 'deaf' or 'mute', a translation of an Arabic term asamm, 'deaf', used for irrational numbers.
common_mistakes: Confusing surd with absurd or sword, which are different words with different sounds.
Using surd for any root, when it refers specifically to irrational roots.

surd.etymology: from Latin *surdus* (“deaf, mute”), used in mathematics for “irrational,” reflecting *ἄλογος* (“irrational, speechless”) as found in Euclid, apparently transmitted via Arabic *جِذْر أَصَمّ* (“deaf root”).

senses.definition: One who survives, especially one who survives a traumatic experience.
senses.example: From this moment on, I choose to live not as a victim, but as a survivor.

senses.definition: A person who is able to endure hardship.
One who knew a specific decedent.
senses.example: She was from a large family and had many friends, so the funeral was crowded with mourning survivors.

core.definition: A person who remains alive after an accident, attack, or disaster, or who has come through a serious illness or hardship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VY, and the final -or is a reduced ur sound, not a full OR. Keep the first syllable light.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful; it admires resilience, though it can sound heavy when linked to trauma.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use survivor for people who lived through accidents, illnesses, or abuse, as in 'cancer survivor' or 'abuse survivor'. In everyday talk it can be affectionate, as in 'You're a survivor!' At a funeral, survivors means the family and friends left behind.

distinctions.note: Victim focuses on the harm done to someone, while survivor focuses on living through it and often sounds more empowering.
Survival is the state or act of staying alive, while a survivor is the person who did it.

examples.everyday: She is a cancer survivor, and she organizes a charity walk every spring to raise money for research.
examples.professional: We track survivors of the onboarding process, meaning customers who completed every setup step.
examples.analytical: A survivor's story is not always a reliable guide to what caused an event, since those who died cannot tell theirs.

nuance.analogy: A survivor is like a boat that came through the storm: battered and scarred, but still afloat.
nuance.etymology: From survive, from Latin supervivere 'to live beyond,' with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Using survivor for someone who simply lived a long life, such as a grandmother who reached 90; the word implies danger or hardship.
Confusing survivor (a person) with survival (the state of staying alive), as in 'the survivor of the disaster' versus 'the survival of the disaster'.

senses.definition: A seam formed by sewing two edges together, especially to join pieces of skin in surgically treating a wound.
senses.example: The surgeon used fine thread to close the cut with twelve neat sutures.

senses.definition: Thread used to sew or stitch two edges (especially of skin) together.

The procedure by which a subject comes to be identified with its own representation, as in the identification of the speaker with the sign “I” within a certain discourse; any process by which the content of something is determined or supplied from outside itself.
senses.example: In Lacanian theory, the subject's suture into discourse happens when the speaker says I.

senses.definition: An area where separate terrane join together along a major fault.
senses.example: The mountain belt marks a suture where two terranes collided along an ancient fault zone.

senses.definition: A type of fibrous joint bound together by Sharpey's fibres which only occurs in the skull.
senses.example: The sutures of the skull fuse gradually, so the infant's head remains soft for months.

senses.definition: A seam or line, such as that between the segments of a crustacean, between the whorls of a univalve shell, or where the elytra of a beetle meet.
senses.example: The beetle's elytra meet along a visible suture running down the middle of its back.

senses.definition: The seam at the union of two margins in a plant.
senses.example: Along the fruit's suture, the pod splits open to release its seeds in late summer.

senses.definition: To sew up or join by means of a suture.
senses.example: The doctor sutured the gash on his hand before he left the clinic.

core.definition: A seam made by sewing the edges of a wound together, or the thread used to do it.
